title: Pushed drugmakers into direct-to-consumer sales and TrumpRx while Trump Jr. sat on the board of BlinkRx, which sells that service

business_entity.name: BlinkRx
business_entity.family_stake: Donald Trump Jr. joined BlinkRx's board of directors in February 2025, according to the company's announcement as cited by congressional Democrats and CREW. Before that, 1789 Capital, the venture firm where he is a partner, led BlinkRx's $140 million Series D financing round in 2024. The size of 1789 Capital's stake and any board compensation are not public.

government_nexus.action: On July 31, 2025, President Trump sent letters to 17 drugmakers pressing them to sell drugs directly to consumers; on September 30, 2025, he announced TrumpRx.gov, a government website, launched February 5, 2026, that routes patients to drugmakers' direct-sale sites.
government_nexus.note: BlinkRx sells drugmakers exactly the service the policy asks of them: a week after the July letters it launched a program promising to set up a direct-to-patient sales channel in 21 days. The Wall Street Journal reported that before TrumpRx was announced, a BlinkRx representative told a drug company BlinkRx could be involved in running the site for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, and that BlinkRx planned a December summit for drugmakers with cabinet officials ending at Trump Jr.'s private club. BlinkRx told lawmakers it learned of TrumpRx from press reports and had no role in it; no public record shows BlinkRx running TrumpRx or being named a TrumpRx partner.

status: Ongoing, unresolved: TrumpRx launched in February 2026 and added Amazon Pharmacy, GoodRx and Cost Plus Drugs in May; no public record shows a BlinkRx role. An ethics group's December 2025 complaint and senators' January 2026 letter to HHS's inspector general have no public answer found.
date_of_action: 2024 (1789 Capital leads BlinkRx's $140 million Series D round; backstory) through 2026-05-18 (TrumpRx expands through Amazon Pharmacy, GoodRx and Cost Plus Drugs, with no BlinkRx role announced)
what_changed:
Backstory: in 2024, 1789 Capital, the venture firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, led a $140 million Series D financing round for BlinkRx, an online pharmacy that delivers prescription drugs and helps drugmakers sell directly to patients. In February 2025, BlinkRx named Trump Jr. to its board of directors.

On July 31, 2025, President Trump sent letters to 17 pharmaceutical companies pressing them to lower drug costs through direct-to-consumer sales. About a week later, on August 7, BlinkRx launched "Operation Access Now," a service it promoted to drugmakers to stand up direct-to-patient programs in as little as 21 days. Several days before the administration announced TrumpRx, the Wall Street Journal later reported, a BlinkRx representative "told one drug company that BlinkRx could be involved with running the site on behalf of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services." On September 30, 2025, the President announced TrumpRx, a government website planned for 2026 that would steer patients to buy drugs directly from manufacturers, alongside a pricing deal with Pfizer; AstraZeneca and Amgen soon said their direct-sale programs would also be reachable through it.

On October 7, 2025, the Wall Street Journal reported that BlinkRx and 1789 Capital would host a "Future of Pharmaceuticals" summit in early December at the Four Seasons in Washington, where top drugmakers were "set to meet" with Trump Jr. and senior administration officials, with Pfizer, Eli Lilly and Amgen invited, "small group meetings" with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and FDA Commissioner Marty Makary on the agenda, and a closing dinner at the Executive Branch, the private club Trump Jr. co-founded. BlinkRx's vice president of corporate affairs said "no company will be pitching any services" at the event; Trump Jr. called the report an "innuendo smear"; and a Trump spokesperson denied BlinkRx had received favorable treatment, saying, "As long as drugmakers deliver cost savings for American patients through TrumpRx, how they do so is irrelevant." On October 23, 2025, the top Democrats on the House Energy and Commerce, House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees, Reps. Frank Pallone Jr. and Richard Neal and Sen. Ron Wyden, wrote to BlinkRx's CEO, saying the timing of its launch and the President's son's role "raises questions about potential coordination, influence, and self-dealing," and asked whether anyone from BlinkRx had discussed the TrumpRx announcement with the administration and whether Trump Jr. had ever recused himself from a board matter. BlinkRx replied that it first learned about TrumpRx "from press reports" and had "no role in the development" of the announcement, according to CREW.

On December 5, 2025, the ethics group Democracy Defenders Fund filed a complaint asking HHS's Office of Inspector General to investigate whether BlinkRx received material nonpublic information that gave it an edge in a possible bid to run TrumpRx. A trade publication later reported that the December summit was postponed because of scheduling problems from the government shutdown. Common Dreams wrote in February 2026 that Trump Jr. "reportedly met" drug company executives and administration officials at a gathering hosted by BlinkRx, but it cited only the Journal's October preview of the planned event; no account of the summit taking place was found.

On January 29, 2026, two days after HHS's inspector general issued guidance the department said "clears [the] path" for TrumpRx, Sens. Dick Durbin, Elizabeth Warren and Peter Welch asked the inspector general for more review before launch, citing "possible conflicts of interest" in "the potential relationship between TrumpRx and an online dispensing company, BlinkRx," and asking whether the office had communicated with any BlinkRx representative, including Trump Jr. On January 30, CREW reported that BlinkRx was one of three companies that added Trump Jr. to their boards after the election and may benefit from his father's administration, while noting it found no evidence of "a clear quid pro quo." TrumpRx launched on February 5, 2026, linking users to drugmakers' own direct-sale sites, such as AstraZeneca Direct. On May 18, 2026, the President announced that more than 600 generic drugs were being added to TrumpRx through partnerships with Amazon Pharmacy, GoodRx and Mark Cuban's Cost Plus Drugs; BlinkRx was not among the partners named. No public answer from the inspector general to the complaint or the senators' letter was found.

financial_stake.summary: No public figure shows any BlinkRx revenue from TrumpRx or from drugmakers' new direct-sale programs, or what Trump Jr. holds or earns at BlinkRx. The public money figure is the $140 million round that 1789 Capital, his venture firm, led in BlinkRx in 2024; the family interest is the value of that stake and his board seat if the policy grows BlinkRx's business.

figures.source: Letter from Reps. Pallone and Neal and Sen. Wyden to BlinkRx CEO Geoffrey Chaiken (Oct. 23, 2025)

financial_stake.caveat: The $140 million figure is the round's total, not 1789 Capital's share, and neither the stake nor Trump Jr.'s board pay is disclosed. The claim that BlinkRx could help run TrumpRx rests on the Wall Street Journal's account of one drug company's conversation; it was not confirmed by any document found, and TrumpRx's later partners were other companies. BlinkRx says it learned of TrumpRx from press reports and had no role in developing it, and that no company would pitch services at its summit; an industry analyst quoted by the Journal said BlinkRx is "one of many companies" offering these services, the difference being that "Trump's son is on the board." Trump Jr. calls the reporting an "innuendo smear," and the White House says that as long as drugmakers deliver savings through TrumpRx, "how they do so is irrelevant." The administration presents direct-to-consumer sales and TrumpRx as a way to cut drug prices.

legal_context: Lawful-but-concerning conduct as reported; no violation has been found and no one has been charged. The President is excluded from the federal criminal conflict-of-interest statute, 18 U.S.C. 208 (by 18 U.S.C. 202(c)), and no rule bars his son from sitting on the board of a company that may benefit from a policy. Democracy Defenders Fund's complaint invokes the Standards of Ethical Conduct for Employees of the Executive Branch (5 C.F.R. part 2635) and federal contracting law, asking whether BlinkRx received nonpublic information; that is the group's allegation, not a finding. Separately, Sens. Durbin, Warren and Welch asked HHS's inspector general whether TrumpRx and the drugmaker platforms it links to comply with the federal Anti-Kickback Statute (42 U.S.C. 1320a-7b(b)); that concern is about TrumpRx generally, not a finding against BlinkRx.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the public record: Trump Jr.'s February 2025 board seat, 1789 Capital's lead role in the $140 million round, the August 2025 BlinkRx launch, the TrumpRx announcement and launch, and the lawmakers' and ethics group's letters come from the letters themselves, CREW and contemporaneous news reports. MODERATE on the claim that a BlinkRx representative pitched a role running TrumpRx: it rests on the Wall Street Journal's reporting (paywalled; read through Media Matters, the Daily Beast and CREW), and BlinkRx denies any role. Unclear: whether the December 2025 summit took place; a trade report says it was postponed, and a later Common Dreams line saying Trump Jr. "reportedly met" executives and officials there cites only the Journal's October preview. No record shows any official attending. No public figure shows BlinkRx revenue from the policy, and no record found shows BlinkRx running or partnering with TrumpRx. Frame as a documented appearance of conflict, not proven favoritism.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of a pattern TAP documents in which companies that brought the President's eldest son onto their boards, or that his venture firm backed, stand to gain from his father's policies. The administration's drug-pricing claims themselves are tracked in the most-favored-nation drug pricing entry; Trump Jr.'s private club, where BlinkRx's summit was to end, is tracked in the Executive Branch club entry; the federal awards to other 1789 Capital companies are tracked in the sons' defense-tech portfolio entry; and the GrabAGun entry covers another 1789 Capital company with Trump Jr. on its board that stands to gain from a pending federal rule. This entry differs in that the benefit runs through a consumer-health policy rather than a contract: BlinkRx sells the service the policy asks drugmakers to adopt.
pull_quote: Drug-industry analyst Adam Fein to the Wall Street Journal: "BlinkRx is one of many companies in the marketplace that provide these kinds of services to manufacturers. What is different is Trump's son is on the board."

glance.what: Pushed direct drug sales and TrumpRx while Trump Jr. sat on the board of BlinkRx, which sells that service

section_summaries.what_changed: As Trump pushed drugmakers into direct sales and TrumpRx, BlinkRx, with Trump Jr. on its board, sold that service; no BlinkRx role in TrumpRx has been shown.
section_summaries.financial_stake: No public figure shows BlinkRx revenue from the policy or Trump Jr.'s stake; his firm 1789 Capital led a $140M round in BlinkRx in 2024.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Board seat, funding round, launch timing and letters are on the record; a pitched TrumpRx role rests on WSJ reporting, and BlinkRx denies any role.

title: Trump pardoned his daughter's father-in-law Charles Kushner, then made him ambassador to France

business_entity.name: Kushner Companies
business_entity.family_stake: Charles Kushner founded Kushner Companies, a New Jersey-based real estate firm, in 1985 and became its chairman; AP describes him as the firm's founder. His son Jared Kushner is married to Ivanka Trump. Kushner's current ownership share in the firm is not public.

government_nexus.action: Trump's full and unconditional pardon of Charles Kushner on December 23, 2020, followed by Trump's 2025 nomination of Kushner as U.S. Ambassador to France and Monaco, which the Senate confirmed 51-45 on May 19, 2025.
government_nexus.note: The link is a family tie, not a business deal: Trump used two presidential powers, clemency and appointment, for the same person, the father of his son-in-law Jared Kushner. No official act benefiting Kushner Companies has been reported. A pardon restores legal standing but does not erase the underlying conduct from public scrutiny, and the family relationship raises a nepotism concern separate from whether the pardon itself was proper.

status: Serving as U.S. Ambassador to France and Monaco since July 2025. France cut his direct access to its ministers on February 23, 2026 after he skipped a summons; after he called the foreign minister, CNN reported on February 27 that his access had been restored.
date_of_action: 2025-05-19 (Senate confirms Kushner as ambassador) through 2026-02-27 (France cuts Kushner's direct access to ministers after he skips a February 23 summons; CNN reports it restored by February 27)
what_changed: Backstory: Charles Kushner, father of Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner, pleaded guilty in 2004 to 18 felony counts including tax evasion, making illegal campaign contributions, and witness retaliation -- **the retaliation count stemmed from Kushner hiring a prostitute to seduce his brother-in-law (a cooperating witness against him) and sending a video of the encounter to his own sister**. Trump pardoned Kushner in December 2020, during his first term's final weeks. In 2025, Trump nominated Kushner to serve as U.S. Ambassador to France and Monaco. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Kushner acknowledged the underlying conduct as a 'serious mistake.' On May 19, 2025, the Senate confirmed Kushner by a vote of 51-45, with Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ) breaking with nearly all Democratic colleagues to vote in favor, and Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) voting against confirmation despite being a Republican. Kushner was sworn in on July 11, 2025. As ambassador he has twice been summoned by France's foreign ministry: in August 2025 over a letter he wrote to President Emmanuel Macron alleging France was not doing enough to combat antisemitism, which the ministry called "unacceptable" (he sent his deputy instead of appearing), and in February 2026 over State Department and U.S. Embassy posts blaming "violent radical leftism" for the beating death of far-right activist Quentin Deranque in Lyon. When Kushner skipped the February 23, 2026 meeting, the foreign ministry said Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot had requested that he "no longer have direct access to members of the French government"; the next morning Barrot said the no-show would "naturally, affect his capacity to exercise his mission in our country" and that he would regain access once explanations had been given. Kushner called Barrot the next day; Barrot's office said he "expressed his willingness not to interfere in our public debate," and the two agreed to meet, according to the Associated Press. By February 27, a French foreign ministry spokesman said Kushner had given assurances that he had not meant to interfere in "the internal sphere of France," and CNN reported that his access to the French government had been restored.

financial_stake.summary: No money is reported to have flowed to a family business from the pardon or the appointment. The stake is the post itself and the family tie: Kushner is a wealthy real estate developer who founded Kushner Companies and has donated significant amounts to Trump's campaigns, and the Paris embassy is a post usually given to a major donor or close ally of the president.
financial_stake.caveat: There are no dollar figures to weigh here. Trump praised Kushner as "a tremendous business leader, philanthropist and dealmaker" when he named him, and his 2020 pardon cited Kushner's record of "reform" and "charity". Kushner told senators "I made a very, very, very serious mistake" and argued his past made him "more qualified to do this job." Supporters can also argue the conduct is two decades old, that he served his sentence, that a pardon is meant to allow full reintegration including public service, and that choosing ambassadors is a legitimate presidential prerogative.

legal_context: Both acts rest on constitutional presidential powers: the pardon on the Pardon Clause (U.S. Const. art. II, sec. 2, cl. 1) and the ambassadorship on the Appointments Clause (art. II, sec. 2, cl. 2), which the Senate exercised by confirming him. Neither has been found unlawful, and no legal challenge has been reported. This is lawful-but-concerning conduct: the concern is pairing a pardon with a prestigious post for a member of the president's extended family whose crimes included retaliating against a federal witness.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the underlying conviction, the 2020 pardon, the nomination, the hearing testimony and the confirmation vote breakdown are all well-documented public record, corroborated across The Hill, Reuters and AP reporting. What is disputed is the characterization: critics see the pardon-then-appointment sequence as a reward for family ties, while Trump and Senate supporters treat it as a legitimate use of two presidential powers for a rehabilitated businessman. There is no public figure for any financial benefit, and no reporting ties the appointment to a Kushner Companies business interest. The August 2025 and February 2026 summonses, Barrot's statements and the February 24 call rest on the Associated Press (via NPR); the February 23 ministry statement cutting his direct access and the restoration of that access by February 27 rest on CNN. No later reporting on the dispute was found.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern this database documents of Trump using both pardon power and appointment power to reward personal loyalty and family connections, sometimes in combination (a pardon followed by a prestigious appointment for the same individual), rather than as fully independent exercises of each power.
pull_quote: At his 2025 confirmation hearing, Kushner called his criminal past, which included a video-blackmail scheme against a cooperating witness, a “very, very, very serious mistake.”

section_summaries.what_changed: Senate confirmed Charles Kushner, pardoned in 2020 for crimes including witness retaliation, as France ambassador; in Feb. 2026 France briefly cut his access after he skipped a summons.
section_summaries.financial_stake: No business payoff is reported; the stake is a prized diplomatic post given to a family member and campaign donor whom Trump had pardoned.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Well documented public record in The Hill, Reuters and AP; disputed only in how the pardon-then-appointment sequence is read.

title: FIFA leased a mostly empty Trump Tower office from the Trump Organization while Trump chaired the White House World Cup task force

business_entity.name: Trump Organization
business_entity.family_stake: The landlord is Trump Tower Commercial LLC, which owns and manages Trump Tower and which Le Monde reports is chaired by Eric Trump (as reported by FootballTransfers and Hoodline). Eric Trump hosted the July 2025 office opening as the Trump Organization's executive vice president, saying "On behalf of myself, on behalf of New York, on behalf of the Trump Organization and everybody that works in this building -- we love you" (FIFA media release). The New York Times reported in June 2026 that "the rent goes to President Trump's family business."

government_nexus.action: Trump chairs the White House Task Force on the FIFA World Cup 2026, created by Executive Order 14234 on March 7, 2025, a coordinated federal effort, housed in the Department of Homeland Security, to support the 2026 World Cup FIFA staged in U.S. cities; Infantino also credited it with supporting FIFA's 2025 Club World Cup. In December 2025, days after FIFA gave Trump its new peace prize, the Justice Department moved to drop its reinstated FIFA bribery convictions of Hernan Lopez and Full Play Group; a judge dismissed the case on May 27, 2026. During the 2026 World Cup, Trump called FIFA President Gianni Infantino about U.S. striker Folarin Balogun's red card, which FIFA then reversed.

official.name: Donald Trump
official.role: President; Chair, White House Task Force on the FIFA World Cup 2026

also_officials.name: Andrew Giuliani
also_officials.role: Executive Director, White House Task Force on the FIFA World Cup 2026

also_officials.name: Joseph Nocella
also_officials.role: U.S. Attorney, Eastern District of New York

government_nexus.note: FIFA needed federal support to host two tournaments in the United States, which Trump's task force was created to coordinate; at the office opening Infantino thanked Trump and "the White House Task Force" for their support. FIFA's rent goes to the Trump family's company. House Judiciary Democrats allege the lease and the peace prize were favors meant to win the bribery-case dismissal and federal inaction on World Cup ticket pricing. No official finding links the lease to any government decision: DOJ said the case did not fit its priorities, Bloomberg Law reported Sauer believed he would lose it at the Supreme Court, and Trump and Infantino deny any pressure over Balogun.

status: FIFA has paid rent since June 2025 on a roughly $4 million lease running more than seven years for a Trump Tower office reported to sit mostly empty. FIFA says the rent is at market rate. House Judiciary Democrats are investigating; no official body has found a quid pro quo.
date_of_action: 2025-03-07 (Trump creates the White House World Cup task force, which he chairs) through 2026-10-13 (The New York Times and Le Monde report the Trump Tower lease's terms)
what_changed: On March 7, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14234 creating the White House Task Force on the FIFA World Cup 2026, with himself as chair and Vice President JD Vance as vice chair; on May 6 he named Andrew Giuliani its executive director. In May 2025, according to Le Monde, four FIFA board members including Secretary General Mattias Grafstrom signed a lease under which FIFA's Delaware subsidiary, FIFA Americas Inc., would pay Trump Tower Commercial LLC, the company that owns and manages Trump Tower, from June 2025. Le Monde reported that, unlike for its Miami offices, FIFA ran no tender and considered no other properties. On July 8, 2025, ahead of the July 13 Club World Cup final in New Jersey, FIFA announced the office at a Trump Tower ceremony where Infantino and Eric Trump unveiled the tournament trophy for a five-day display in the building. Infantino said "we are opening an office of FIFA here in Trump Tower. Thank you, Eric," and thanked Trump and "the White House Task Force" for their support. **On December 5, 2025, at the World Cup draw at the Kennedy Center, Infantino gave Trump the first "FIFA Peace Prize," which FIFA had announced in November, telling him "This is your prize, this is your peace prize";** Human Rights Watch said FIFA had not answered its request for the nominees, judges and selection process. On December 9, at Solicitor General John Sauer's direction, U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella moved to dismiss with prejudice the FIFA bribery convictions of former Fox executive Hernan Lopez and Argentine marketing firm Full Play Group, which an appeals court had reinstated that July; Bloomberg Law noted the reversal came days after the peace prize. The FIFA Ethics Committee acknowledged a complaint from rights group FairSquare against Infantino on December 12. On May 27, 2026, Judge Pamela Chen dismissed the case after Nocella said it "doesn't fit with the administration's priorities." On June 9, 2026, as the World Cup opened, The New York Times reported that the Trump Tower office had "sat all but empty" for a year. During the tournament Trump called Infantino about U.S. striker Folarin Balogun's red card before the July 6 round-of-16 match against Belgium, and FIFA reversed it; both men deny any pressure. On July 27, House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin wrote to Infantino alleging "outright bribery," demanding records of anything of value FIFA gave Trump or his companies and visitor logs for the Trump Tower office, and asking Infantino to sit for a transcribed interview. After the tournament Infantino dropped a plan to sell a stake in FIFA competitions to private investors that, The New Republic reported, included Josh Kushner, brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner. On September 8, FairSquare announced a follow-up ethics complaint, and Norway's football federation has filed three ethics complaints, over the peace prize, the Balogun reversal and the private-investor plan. On September 23, The Athletic reported that FIFA had not turned over the priority documents Raskin requested or made Infantino available, though its U.S. lawyers had held a Capitol Hill briefing on his questions on August 19; a Democratic spokesperson called FIFA's cooperation "woefully inadequate," and FIFA said its talks with House staff had been productive. On October 13, 2026, The New York Times and Le Monde reported the lease's terms: about $4 million over seven years and seven months for a roughly 450-square-meter 17th-floor suite that mostly sits empty, used mainly for special events and during the U.N. General Assembly, with no plans to fully staff it. Two officials told the Times that Infantino drove the decision over concerns from senior FIFA officials. FIFA says the lease "complies with all local laws" and followed its standard internal processes; the White House declined to comment.

financial_stake.summary: FIFA pays the Trump family's company about $4 million over seven years and seven months, starting June 2025, for a Trump Tower suite that mostly sits empty. FIFA, in turn, ran a World Cup that relied on federal support coordinated by Trump's task force, and saw DOJ drop two convictions from its FIFA bribery probe, which House Judiciary Democrats say uncovered over $200 million in bribes.

financial_stake.caveat: The lease value and terms come from documents and officials cited by The New York Times and Le Monde; the full lease is not public, and the roughly $15,000-per-day figure Courthouse News attributes to Raskin's letter is far above what the Times total implies; its basis is not explained in the coverage read. The rent's flow to the Trump family beyond the landlord company is not itemized publicly. FIFA says the rent is at market rate, the lease complies with local law and was signed under its standard processes, and that a New York presence is logical for a global body. DOJ said the Lopez and Full Play dismissal was limited to that case and reflected enforcement priorities. The White House called the World Cup a historic success it delivered and called Raskin "a stupid person's idea of a smart person" without addressing his claims.

legal_context: FIFA is a private Swiss association, not a foreign state, so rent it pays the Trump Organization is not clearly a payment covered by the Foreign Emoluments Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, sec. 9, cl. 8). The main federal conflict-of-interest statute, 18 U.S.C. sec. 208, does not apply to the President (18 U.S.C. sec. 202(c)). Rep. Raskin describes the lease and peace prize as "outright bribery" (the federal bribery statute is 18 U.S.C. sec. 201), but no prosecutor or court has made any such finding, and House Democrats, in the minority, cannot compel Infantino to testify. As documented, the arrangement is lawful-but-concerning: a body seeking federal help pays rent to the president's family company.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence that FIFA opened an office in Trump Tower in July 2025 with Eric Trump, that Trump chairs the task force, that FIFA gave Trump its peace prize and that DOJ dropped the Lopez and Full Play case: each is in FIFA's own release, the executive order, wire reports or court reporting. MEDIUM-HIGH on the lease terms and on how little the office is used, which rest on documents and officials cited by The New York Times and Le Monde (read here through partial and secondary copies) and which FIFA does not dispute except to call the rent market-rate. LOW on any causal link between the lease and an official act: the quid pro quo claim is House Democrats' allegation, and DOJ, Trump and Infantino give other reasons for each decision.

title: Trump Jr.'s ex-fiancee Kimberly Guilfoyle, made ambassador to Greece, was ousted after reports she sought $100,000 from a donor and took Greek tycoons' gifts

business_entity.name: Guilfoyle's private speaking and consulting work (payments sought from donor Eric Deters)
business_entity.family_stake: Guilfoyle's own business. Donor Eric Deters told The Wall Street Journal he paid her $300,000 over the years to speak at his Freedom Fest event (and paid speaking fees of $200,000 to Donald Trump Jr. and $100,000 to Eric Trump), and Deters told the Journal she asked him to describe two $50,000 back payments as money owed for consulting. Her February 2025 financial disclosure listed a medspa and a vodka company, each worth $1 million to $5 million, and nearly $800,000 in podcast income.

government_nexus.action: Trump's appointment of Guilfoyle as U.S. Ambassador to Greece (named December 10, 2024; confirmed by the Senate 51-47 on September 18, 2025) and her conduct as nominee and ambassador, which ended when the White House asked her to resign on October 13, 2026.
government_nexus.note: The reported conflict has two halves. Before confirmation, according to messages reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, she sought money from a donor while lobbying the IRS commissioner on his behalf, invoking her closeness to Donald Trump Jr.; she says he owed her for speeches. As ambassador, the Journal reported, she promoted Greek firm Aktor Group to governments across southeastern Europe while flying on its CEO's private jet and including its lobbyist in official meetings, and a Greek shipping executive reportedly paid for her Paris hotel stay. Her lawyers and the embassy say she followed State Department ethics, gift and travel guidance.

status: Resigned October 13, 2026, at the White House's request; she denies all the allegations. The State Department inspector general is reported to be examining them, D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro is waiting on that review, and donor Eric Deters sued her for defamation on October 15.
date_of_action: 2024-12-10 (Trump names Guilfoyle his pick for ambassador to Greece) through 2026-10-15 (donor Eric Deters sues her in Kenton County, Kentucky)
what_changed: Backstory: Eric Deters, a Trump donor and former Kentucky congressional candidate, says he had paid Kimberly Guilfoyle $300,000 over the years to speak at his Freedom Fest event, and after Trump's election win he sought her help getting the new administration's attention on an IRS inquiry into his taxes and a Justice Department extradition request, promising payments of as much as $1 million if she succeeded, according to Deters and messages reviewed by The Wall Street Journal. On December 10, 2024, Trump named Guilfoyle, Donald Trump Jr.'s former fiancee, as his pick for U.S. ambassador to Greece. Her contacts with Deters grew more frequent after the nomination; in January 2025 she scolded him for mentioning their arrangement to a podcast producer, writing "Do not say we have any arrangement" and "you'll literally cost me my ambassadorship." In June 2025 she sent IRS Commissioner Billy Long Deters' letter on his tax dispute, writing "Don Jr. and I are very close with Eric Deters and his wife." **On July 3, 2025, six days before her July 9 Senate confirmation hearing, she sent Deters American Express payment instructions; as the hearing approached she wrote, "It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," according to the Journal; Deters did not pay.** The Senate confirmed her 51-47 on September 18, 2025. She flew to Athens in November on a private jet with Greek American businessman Eric Vassilatos, people familiar told the Journal, and presented her credentials on November 4. In January 2026 she flew to the World Economic Forum in Davos on a private jet with Alexandros Exarchou, chief executive of Greek construction firm Aktor Group; on an audio recording reviewed by the Journal she pressed to get into a dinner for Eric Trump and said she would be flying to Paris with shipping executive Nikolas Tsakos, with whom she had spent the holidays; Tsakos paid her bill at the Four Seasons Hotel George V, people familiar told the Journal. Through the spring, the Journal reported, she promoted Aktor, whose joint venture with a Greek state-backed company had signed a 20-year deal to buy U.S. liquefied natural gas, to governments across southeastern Europe, from Bulgaria to Albania, with Aktor lobbyist Christos Marafatsos in her meetings; at a March dinner in Athens she allegedly told Greece's energy minister, of Romania's coming government collapse, "We can do that to any country we want," which her lawyer disputes. The Journal began publishing these accounts in late September 2026, and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen and Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrats on the Senate and House foreign affairs committees, wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio asking for a review. The Journal published the Deters messages on October 7, while Rubio was in Athens calling her "a strong ambassador," and the Davos recording on October 10. On October 12 Trump said of firing her, "We're looking at it. We're not happy," and Deters said he would sue her and her lawyers for defamation after they called his texts fake. On October 13 the White House said it had asked her to resign; she did so the same day, calling the allegations "false." Trump said she "was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading" and that she "wasn't a member of my family." Pirro said she would wait for the State Department inspector general. On October 15 Deters sued Guilfoyle and several of her lawyers in Kenton County, Kentucky, alleging defamation, false light and breach of contract; he wants to depose Guilfoyle and Donald Trump Jr., though no deposition of Trump Jr. has been ordered.

financial_stake.summary: The money in question is personal, not a family company's: a $100,000 credit card balance Guilfoyle allegedly asked a donor to pay before her confirmation, up to $1 million he says he promised for her help, and free private-jet travel and luxury lodging reportedly given by Greek businessmen, one of them the chief executive of Aktor, a firm the Journal reported she promoted. Aktor paid its lobbyist $160,000 through June 2026.

financial_stake.caveat: The $100,000 request, the $1 million promise and the $300,000 in fees come from Deters and from messages he gave the Journal; Guilfoyle's lawyer disputes the messages' authenticity without specifics and says Deters owed her for speaking events and consulting, which Deters denies. No dollar value has been reported for the jet travel or the Paris hotel stay. Her lawyers say she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance" on her travel, and the Athens embassy says she "faithfully followed State Department ethics and gift reporting guidelines." Aktor's lawyer says she "has been consistently promoting U.S. interests," and the deal she promoted would buy American gas. Before her ouster Rubio called her an "incredibly effective advocate for the President's agenda."

legal_context: As an executive branch employee, an ambassador is bound by the Standards of Ethical Conduct (5 C.F.R. part 2635), which limit gifts from outside sources (subpart B) and bar using public office for private gain or to endorse a private enterprise (subpart G); State Department rules also required her to get approval before flying on private aircraft. Whether her travel and her promotion of Aktor complied is what the State Department inspector general is reported to be examining; her lawyers and the embassy say she followed the guidance. Deters calls the $100,000 request a quid pro quo. The federal bribery statute (18 U.S.C. sec. 201) covers people already nominated to office, but no prosecutor is reported to have opened a case or charged her: D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said she would wait for the inspector general. No violation of any of these rules has been found; every account of misconduct here remains an allegation she denies.
confidence_note: MEDIUM-HIGH confidence on the core facts: her appointment, confirmation and forced resignation, Trump's and the White House's comments, the congressional letters and the reported inspector general review are on the record across NBC News, CNN, CNBC, AP and NPR. The misconduct accounts rest mainly on The Wall Street Journal's reporting, its review of Deters' messages and an audio recording, and people familiar with her travel; other outlets have not independently confirmed them, and Guilfoyle denies them all and disputes the messages' authenticity. Deters is a partisan source with a disciplinary record and is now suing her. Trump disputes that she was family; she was engaged to Donald Trump Jr. from 2020 until their 2024 split, and she invoked that tie in her outreach to the IRS commissioner.

title: Kushner-backed Albania resorts won fast-track status from Rama's government, then drew a land-fraud probe and mass protests while he serves as U.S. envoy

business_entity.name: Atlantic Incubation Partners and Sazan Real Estate Development (Kushner-backed Albania resort group)
business_entity.family_stake: Jared Kushner announced the Albania plans in 2024 as an Affinity Partners project (MS NOW), but Affinity's PR agency later said Affinity is neither an investor nor the developer and that the partners invest in a personal capacity (Exit.al). Kushner calls himself a minority partner not involved in day-to-day management (Tirana Times); Sazan Real Estate Development has confirmed he is an investor, but his role and the size of his investment have not been made public (Reuters). Ivanka Trump has publicly described the resort as her and her husband's plan (CBS News), saying "We developed the opportunity," and made a January 2026 site visit (The New Republic); no stake of her own has been reported.

government_nexus.action: Albania's Strategic Investment Committee, chaired by Prime Minister Edi Rama, granted the Kushner-linked Atlantic Incubation Partners strategic-investor status for a €1.4 billion resort on state-owned Sazan Island on December 30, 2024, giving it fast-track procedures and access to state land and state-funded infrastructure; a February 2024 law had opened protected areas to luxury resorts, and Rama's government has championed the larger Zvërnec project on the protected Vjosa-Narta coast.

also_officials.name: Jared Kushner
also_officials.role: Presidential envoy for peace since February 2026 (unpaid; the White House calls him a volunteer)

government_nexus.note: Kushner is seeking a foreign government's approvals for a multi-billion-euro private project while serving as President Trump's envoy for peace, negotiating for the United States on Gaza, Iran and Ukraine (Politico). The Sazan status came three weeks before Trump's inauguration (Exit.al), and critics asked whether Rama's government sought to strengthen ties with the incoming administration (Tirana Times). Rama says talks began before Trump's return and that Kushner was not acting for the U.S. government (MS NOW); the White House says Kushner's 'personal business activities have nothing to do with his diplomatic engagements' (MS NOW). No source reports a U.S. policy decision toward Albania tied to the project.

status: Not yet approved: Kushner said October 8, 2026 the Zvërnec project still needs Albanian regulatory and environmental approval. The land-title probe continues, with about €110 million of sale money frozen; seller Shehu is wanted and denies wrongdoing. Mid-October protests demand Rama resign.
date_of_action: 2024-02 (Albania opens protected areas to luxury resorts) through 2026-10-15 (Rama rejects calls to resign as student-led protests turn violent)
what_changed: Backstory: Kushner says his interest in Albania began in the summer of 2021, when he was a private citizen (Tirana Times). In February 2024, Albania's parliament, led by Rama's Socialist Party, passed Law 21/2024, which lets the National Territory Council permit luxury tourist resorts even in protected landscapes, and by March 2024 Kushner had gone public with plans for two developments in the region, including a resort on Sazan Island (Mother Jones, Exit.al). On December 30, 2024, the Strategic Investment Committee chaired by Rama gave the Kushner-linked Atlantic Incubation Partners strategic-investor status for a €1.4 billion resort on 45 hectares of state-owned Sazan, three weeks before Trump's inauguration (Exit.al). For the larger project on the Zvërnec coast, the developers' land company, Albania Land Development, signed in November 2025 to buy 102.9 hectares from Miami-based businessman Artur Shehu for €5.5 million, then completed the same purchase in April 2026 for €122 million, according to records from Albania's anti-corruption prosecutors reported by Shteg (Exit.al); Trump had named Kushner an envoy for peace in February 2026. Protests began in late May, when developers fenced off the Zvërnec beach and private guards were filmed dragging a protester along a cliff (Politico). On June 1, 2026, SPAK, Albania's special anti-corruption prosecutor, confirmed it had opened an investigation into the 2024 changes to the area's protected status and land ownership (Politico), and on June 2 it froze the bank accounts of Albania Land Development, owned by Qatari businessmen Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat, in a probe of allegedly fraudulent property titles (OCCRP). On June 9 a European Commission spokesperson warned that Albania 'should refrain from action that could undermine the fulfillment of the closing benchmark' of its EU accession talks on the environment (MS NOW), and urged repeal of the protected-areas changes (Politico). On June 12 Rama said negotiations were continuing and dismissed the protests (MS NOW), and the same day SPAK announced arrest warrants for 20 people in a drug-trafficking and money-laundering case; case files dated that day and reviewed by Reuters name Shehu among them, allege the Zvërnec land was 'acquired through the use of forged documents,' and say about €110 million from the sale was frozen in a notary's account (Reuters). The protests, dubbed the 'Flamingo Revolution,' grew into a nationwide movement demanding Rama's resignation, with more than 100,000 people at a June 20 rally in Tirana (Mother Jones). In August the Wall Street Journal reported that villagers had tried to warn Kushner the land had been taken from its owners (Exit.al, MS NOW), and on August 25 Rep. Jamie Raskin, top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, asked Kushner for records on the project, including communications with the U.S. and Albanian governments, to determine whether his conduct should be investigated under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (MS NOW). On September 29 Rama said the project's fate would be decided by an environmental impact assessment, not 'streets and ideology' (Euronews). Responding on October 8 to a New Yorker profile, Kushner said his partners bought the Zvërnec land from a private party for €230 million, called himself a minority partner, and said the project still had to pass all Albanian regulatory and environmental reviews (Tirana Times). Student-led protests against Rama turned violent in Tirana from October 13, and on October 15 Rama rejected calls to resign (AP via NBC News).

financial_stake.summary: Two planned luxury resorts: a €1.4 billion development on state-owned Sazan Island and a Zvërnec coastal project that Kushner values at about €4 billion, on land his partners say they bought for €230 million. Kushner's personal share has never been disclosed, and nothing has been built or approved, so no family profit is known.

financial_stake.caveat: The project values are the developers' and Rama's own estimates (Kushner's €4 billion, the €1.4 billion Sazan figure), not Kushner's stake or profit, which have never been disclosed (Reuters, Exit.al). Land figures differ by source: Kushner cites €230 million for all the land, Exit.al reports €122 million for one 102.9-hectare tract, Reuters about €110 million frozen, and CBS News, citing OCCRP, a frozen account of more than $127 million. SPAK has said its probe 'does not concern any company associated with Mr. Kushner' (CBS News), and Reuters found no indication that investors knew of the suspicions about Shehu, who denies all accusations. Kushner says his interest began in 2021 as a private citizen and the project was not meant to curry favor with Trump; Rama says the deal is private and talks began before Trump's return; the developers say 'the underlying land acquisitions were conducted lawfully' (Reuters); and the White House calls Raskin's request 'the same, tired narrative' (MS NOW).

legal_context: Lawful-but-concerning as far as is known. Rep. Raskin has asked whether Kushner's conduct should be investigated under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (15 U.S.C. sec. 78dd-1 et seq.), which bars U.S. persons from paying foreign officials to obtain business; no investigation, charge or finding has been reported, and Kushner says the land was bought from a private party. The Foreign Emoluments Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, sec. 9, cl. 8) reaches only holders of a U.S. office; Kushner says he is an unpaid volunteer, and a pending CREW lawsuit alleging he holds such an office has not been ruled on. The criminal case is Albanian: SPAK is investigating land titles and the seller, not Kushner or his companies.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the project's scale and approvals, the June 2026 SPAK probe and asset freeze, the EU warning, the scale of the protests, the warrant for Shehu and the Raskin letter, each reported by Politico, OCCRP, Reuters, CBS News, MS NOW or AP. MODERATE confidence on the land-price figures, which come from SPAK files seen by Shteg and Reuters but not published, and which differ by source. Disputed: Kushner, Rama and the White House reject any link between the project and his U.S. role, and Shehu denies all accusations; no source reports a U.S. policy act toward Albania tied to the project. Kushner's personal investment is not public. The Wall Street Journal report on villagers' warnings and an Atlantic report on the July protests could not be read directly and are cited only as relayed by Exit.al and MS NOW.

title: Kushner's Affinity Partners won a free Belgrade lease and a fast-track law for a $500M Trump Tower, then quit as Serbian officials were charged

business_entity.name: Affinity Partners
business_entity.family_stake: Jared Kushner founded and leads Affinity Partners (Semafor; BIRN describes it as owned by him), and the deal ran through Affinity Global Development, a company Kushner set up, which signed the 99-year lease (AP; The New York Times). The hotel was to carry the Trump brand: Eric Trump, who runs the Trump Organization's real estate business, confirmed the deal in January 2025, and Donald Trump Jr., a Trump Organization executive vice president, was helping plan it (The New York Times). No licensing terms have been reported.

government_nexus.action: Serbia's government agreed to give the Kushner-linked company a 99-year lease on the former Yugoslav army headquarters site, its parliament passed a November 2025 special law fast-tracking the project and annulling the site's heritage status, and officials stripped the site's cultural-monument protection in a step prosecutors say rested on a forged document.

also_officials.name: Nikola Selaković
also_officials.role: Minister of Culture of Serbia (charged December 2025; denies the charges)

government_nexus.note: Vučić personally backed the project and said it would be good for Serbia's relations with the United States, at a time when the Trump administration had imposed 35% tariffs on Serbian imports and sanctioned Serbia's Russian-controlled oil supplier; a ruling-party lawmaker said he hoped it would improve ties with the Trump administration. In March 2025 Donald Trump Jr. met Vučić in Belgrade to talk about U.S. foreign aid to Serbia while the family's hotel plans moved ahead; Serbia's foreign minister said the visit "provides great momentum for an excellent start to relations with the new administration," while Trump Jr.'s spokesman said he was there "strictly in his capacity as a podcast host" and discussed nothing relating to Trump Org (The New York Times). Richard Grenell, Trump's first-term Balkans envoy, helped negotiate the deal as Kushner's business partner and was then named an envoy for special missions (The New York Times). The terms (a lease the Times says carried no costs, plus fast-track legislation) went to a firm owned by the sitting president's son-in-law. No source reports a confirmed exchange with any U.S. policy decision, and Kushner is not accused of the forgery.

status: Project withdrawn December 15, 2025. Selaković and the three other officials went on trial in Belgrade's Higher Court in February 2026 and deny the charges; hearings continued through September 2026 with no verdict.
date_of_action: 2024-03 (draft lease terms for the former army headquarters site reported) through 2025-12-15 (prosecutors charge four Serbian officials; Kushner's firm withdraws)
what_changed: Affinity Partners, the investment firm Jared Kushner founded after leaving his White House post, set out to build a roughly $500 million Trump-branded hotel and apartment complex in Belgrade, Serbia, on the site of the former Yugoslav army headquarters -- a building bombed by NATO in 1999 and protected as a cultural monument. (Backstory: Donald Trump first proposed a hotel on the site in 2013, and Kushner revived the idea after his first-term White House job ended, with help from Richard Grenell, Trump's former Balkans envoy and Kushner's business partner, according to The New York Times.) In March 2024 the Times reported a draft agreement giving a Kushner company a 99-year lease on the site at no cost, and in May 2024 the Serbian government of President Aleksandar Vučić approved leasing it for 99 years to Affinity Global Development, a company Kushner set up. In November 2024, a week after Trump won re-election, the government stripped the site of its cultural-monument protection; dozens of experts at the state heritage institute objected that only the institute's own experts could approve that (The New York Times). In January 2025 Kushner announced a partnership with Dubai billionaire Mohamed Alabbar, founder of Emaar and head of Eagle Hills, for a 175-room hotel and 1,500 residences (Semafor), and Eric Trump confirmed the Trump Organization would brand the hotel, saying the deal did not breach the family's pledge against new deals with foreign governments because the hotel contract was with the developer, not the Serbian government (The New York Times). In March 2025, amid mass protests against Vučić, Donald Trump Jr., a Trump Organization executive helping plan the hotel, met Vučić in Belgrade to discuss U.S. foreign aid and interviewed him for his podcast; his spokesman said he "at no point had any discussions with anyone relating to Trump Org" (The New York Times). In May 2025 Serbia's organized-crime prosecutors said Goran Vasić, head of the cultural-monuments agency, had "forged a proposal for a decision to revoke the status of cultural property," and the Times reported he had admitted it to the authorities; by June the case had brought resignations and a criminal charge, and the institute's former deputy director said state intelligence officers had pressured her not to challenge the decision (The New York Times). Vučić's government publicly framed the project as a way to strengthen ties with the Trump administration, which had imposed 35% tariffs on Serbian imports and sanctioned NIS, Serbia's Russian-controlled oil monopoly. In early November 2025 Europa Nostra, ICOMOS and other European heritage bodies called for the withdrawal of a draft special law for the site, and on November 7, 2025 parliament passed it, fast-tracking the project; on November 11 thousands of protesters symbolically formed a human shield around the complex (AP). Serbian organized-crime prosecutors alleged the government's decision removing the site's historic-monument protection rested on a falsified proposal from Serbia's Republic Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, drafted without the Institute's conservation experts; on December 15, 2025 they filed an indictment proposal charging Serbian Culture Minister Nikola Selaković -- a close Vučić ally -- along with three other officials, Vasić among them, with abuse of office and document falsification for their roles in stripping that protection to clear the way for the project. Affinity Partners announced its withdrawal the same day, after a year of public protests against the project, stating that 'out of respect for the people of Serbia and the City of Belgrade, we are withdrawing our application and stepping aside at this time.' The Wall Street Journal, as relayed by BIRN, reported that Kushner gave up the plan after the indictment and due to the protests. Rade Bajić, who had worked on the case at Serbia's organized-crime prosecutor's office, was transferred off it in November 2025 with no explanation (The Record). In October 2026 he said Apple had warned him on August 13, 2026 that his phone had been targeted using "mercenary spyware," and that, "in my opinion, my involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack"; he and Citizen Lab said they could not establish with certainty whether his phone was hacked, and Citizen Lab was still analyzing it (Reuters; The Record). Citizen Lab confirmed a Pegasus infection on the phone of Belgrade University rector Vladan Đokić, who has supported the student protests, but not on Bajić's (N1).

financial_stake.summary: A roughly $500 million hotel, apartment, office and retail complex that Kushner confirmed his company planned to finance, on a central Belgrade site Serbia leased for 99 years, which the draft agreement said could become free ownership. The project was withdrawn in December 2025, so no realized family profit is known.

financial_stake.caveat: The $500 million figure is the project's reported value, not Kushner's stake or profit; the free-lease terms come from a draft agreement a Serbian official gave The New York Times in March 2024, which Kushner did not dispute; he said Serbia would tentatively get 22 percent of the profits (N1), and no final lease text has been reviewed. Kushner denies any wrongdoing and has not been accused of illegal activity (Semafor); the forgery case concerns Serbian officials' own conduct. Affinity Partners said that 'meaningful projects should unite rather than divide, and out of respect for the people of Serbia and the City of Belgrade, we are withdrawing our application and stepping aside at this time' (N1). title: Negotiates for the U.S. while owning Gulf-funded Affinity, with no confirmation or disclosure, CREW alleges

business_entity.name: Affinity Partners
business_entity.family_stake: Jared Kushner launched the investment firm A Fin Management LLC (Affinity Partners) after Trump's first term and is its sole owner, according to CREW's complaint citing Affinity's own SEC Form ADV filing.

government_nexus.action: President Trump named Kushner an "envoy of peace" on February 19, 2026, and Kushner negotiates directly with foreign leaders for the United States on the Israel-Hamas, Russia-Ukraine and U.S.-Iran conflicts and represents U.S. interests on the Board of Peace, without Senate confirmation or a public financial disclosure.

official.name: Jared Kushner
official.role: Presidential envoy for peace (unpaid; says he is a volunteer, not a government official)

also_officials.name: Donald Trump
also_officials.role: President (named Kushner an envoy for peace)

government_nexus.note: Affinity manages money for, and collects fees from, the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE, all three of which sit on the Board of Peace, pledged at least $1 billion each to it, and were involved in the Israel-Hamas negotiations Kushner conducts; CREW says at least Qatar has also mediated U.S.-Iran talks. Affinity is also the largest shareholder in Israel's Phoenix Financial, which CNN found holds stakes in Elbit Systems and at least eight other companies that supply Israel's military, while Kushner negotiates for the U.S. on the Israel-Hamas war; Kushner told Forbes in September 2025 that he kept "a very active dialogue" with Phoenix's leadership, and his attorney told CNN that contact has since significantly reduced. Affinity bought into Phoenix in July 2024, and Israel's insurance regulator approved doubling the stake on January 15, 2025, before Kushner took any role in Trump's second term. CNN "found no indication that Kushner's actions as a diplomat directly affected the investments reviewed." Fellow envoy Steve Witkoff, also unpaid but, AP notes, a formal government employee, filed the Ethics Act disclosure Kushner has not, so the public cannot check Kushner's assurances against his firm's Gulf clients. No court or ethics office has found that any diplomatic act benefited Affinity.

status: Lawsuit pending: CREW filed its complaint in D.C. federal court on October 14, 2026; no government answer or ruling yet. Kushner continues as envoy and has filed no public financial disclosure.
date_of_action: 2026-02-19 (Trump names Kushner an envoy for peace) through 2026-10-14 (CREW files suit)
what_changed: Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and a senior White House adviser in Trump's first term, has represented the United States throughout much of the second term in talks over the wars between Israel and Hamas and between Russia and Ukraine, and in talks with Iran, working alongside Special Envoy Steve Witkoff. On February 19, 2026, Trump announced he was making Kushner a special envoy for peace. The next month the watchdog Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) wrote to the White House Counsel asking that Kushner's public financial disclosure report be collected within the 30 days the rules allow, noting that Witkoff had filed one as a special envoy. CREW says that when it asked the White House and State Department in July for any disclosures Kushner had filed, both said they had none. Kushner has said he is not "technically" a government official but "just a volunteer like other businessmen" who help when asked. At the same time he is the sole owner of Affinity Partners, an investment firm with more than $6 billion under management, about 99% of it from foreign investors including the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates; Forbes estimated Affinity's management fees at about $60 million a year. All three countries sit on the Board of Peace, where Kushner represents U.S. interests. As background, Affinity has been the largest shareholder in Phoenix Financial, Israel's largest insurer, since it doubled its stake, with approval from Israel's insurance regulator, days before Trump's second term began. On July 28, 2026, Affinity sold about a quarter of that stake for about NIS 1.05 billion (about $343 million), keeping 7.4%, worth about $1.08 billion. On October 1, 2026, a CNN investigation of Phoenix's Israeli filings, which cover only part of its portfolio, found that Phoenix holds at least $265 million in Elbit Systems, Israel's largest arms maker, and stakes in at least eight other companies that supply Israel's military, while Kushner negotiates over the war in Gaza. Affinity owns none of those companies directly, and CNN said it "found no indication that Kushner's actions as a diplomat directly affected the investments reviewed." Kushner called the story "deeply misleading," saying he has "no role in deciding what Phoenix buys or sells" and that the investment "dates to before President Trump was re-elected." On October 14, 2026, CREW sued Kushner, Witkoff, Chief of Staff Susan Wiles, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and several offices in federal court in Washington. **The complaint alleges Kushner "holds a continuing position and wields significant government authority without having been confirmed by the Senate and without having filed a single financial disclosure."** It asks the court to bar him from acting as an officer until he is confirmed and to order him to file disclosures; if the court finds he is not an officer, to order disclosures as a government official; and if it finds he is a private citizen, to bar him from exercising government power under the private nondelegation doctrine. Kushner has said he has "never taken a diplomatic action to benefit Affinity" and that his ethics counsel and the White House Counsel's Office confirmed he follows all applicable ethics rules.

financial_stake.summary: Kushner solely owns Affinity Partners, whose assets under management passed $6 billion by the end of 2025, about 99% from foreign investors including the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE. Forbes put its management fees at about $60 million a year. Affinity also holds 7.4% of Israel's Phoenix Financial, worth about $1.08 billion: it bought 4.95% in July 2024, doubled that to 9.9% in January 2025 to become the largest shareholder, and sold about a quarter of its stake for about $343 million in July 2026. Because Kushner has filed no disclosure for his envoy role, what he personally earns from Affinity is not public.

financial_stake.caveat: The asset, ownership and fee figures are CREW's, as cited in its complaint from Affinity's own SEC Form ADV filings, Bloomberg, Forbes and a 2024 letter from Sen. Ron Wyden; Kushner calls Wyden's $157 million fee estimate "false" but has not published another figure, and no filing shows his personal income from Affinity. The Phoenix stake and sale figures are Globes', Calcalist's and JNS's; the defense holdings are from CNN's review of Phoenix's public quarterly filings, which cover only part of its portfolio and leave out retirement accounts and holdings through funds and bonds. CNN found no sign that Kushner's diplomacy directly affected those investments, and Affinity holds none of the nine companies directly. Kushner's attorney says he "never participated in or directed Phoenix's decisions" and had "no involvement" in buying, holding or selling the nine; Kushner calls Phoenix the Israeli equivalent of "Vanguard or Fidelity"; and Phoenix says its shareholder value comes "primarily from operating performance rather than investment returns." Kushner says he has "never taken a diplomatic action to benefit Affinity, [him]self, or any investor," that Affinity's investors have never influenced his diplomatic positions, and that he "raised no additional funds for Affinity Partners since President Trump was elected to his second term." His attorney Chad Mizelle calls the suit "without merit," says CREW lacks standing, and says outside ethics counsel and government ethics attorneys "confirmed that his arrangements comply with applicable ethics requirements"; Kushner takes no salary and pays his own expenses. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly says his "personal business activities have nothing to do with his diplomatic engagements," and a White House official says there is nothing unusual about using a private envoy.

legal_context: CREW's complaint invokes the Appointments Clause (U.S. Const. art. II, sec. 2, cl. 2), which requires officers of the United States who hold a continuing position with significant authority to be appointed by the President with the Senate's advice and consent, and the Ethics in Government Act's public financial disclosure rules (5 U.S.C. secs. 13103-13105), which require covered executive-branch officers and employees, including special government employees above set pay levels, to file within 30 days of taking a position. In the alternative, if Kushner is a private citizen, CREW says his exercise of government power violates the private nondelegation doctrine. These are allegations in a pending civil suit; no court has ruled on them. Kushner and the White House say he is an unpaid volunteer to whom neither requirement applies; if a court agrees, his Gulf-funded business alongside his diplomacy would be lawful but concerning, not a violation.
confidence_note: MODERATE confidence on the legal claim, HIGH on the underlying facts. The complaint is read directly from the filed PDF and the case details from the federal court docket, and the March 2026 CREW letter from CREW's own site. That Kushner holds no Senate confirmation and has filed no disclosure is not disputed; he says the rules do not apply to a volunteer. Affinity's asset and fee figures are as cited in CREW's complaint, drawn from Affinity's SEC filings, Forbes and other reporting. Whether Kushner is an officer is CREW's allegation, untested in court. The Phoenix stake and sale are read from Globes, Calcalist and JNS, and Phoenix's defense holdings from CNN's investigation of Phoenix's partial public filings, which two Israeli forensic accountants reviewed; CNN found no indication that Kushner's diplomacy directly affected those investments, and the January 2025 approval was an Israeli regulatory decision made before he took any role in Trump's second term. Disputed: Kushner, his attorney and the White House say he is an unpaid volunteer, not a government official, that his arrangements were reviewed and found compliant by ethics counsel, and that his business has nothing to do with his diplomacy; Kushner and his attorney say he plays no part in Phoenix's investment choices; Kushner disputes Sen. Wyden's fee estimate. Re-verified 2026-10-17: the docket shows no government answer or ruling, and AP and NBC News reporting adds the responses of Kushner's attorney and the White House.

title: Amazon paid $40 million, its most ever for a documentary, for Melania Trump's film, most of it reportedly to her, while the company had business before the Trump administration

business_entity.name: "Melania" film and docuseries, licensed to Amazon MGM Studios
business_entity.family_stake: Melania Trump is the project's executive producer; the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that her cut is "more than 70% of the $40 million" Amazon paid to license the film and a follow-up series. Five Democratic lawmakers estimate her share at roughly $28 million. The President's 2025 financial disclosure lists a $10.71 million licensing fee for "Melania" as 2025 income; neither the First Lady's office nor Amazon has published the full terms.

government_nexus.action: While Amazon had interests before the administration (an FTC monopolization suit, a settled FTC Prime case, cloud contracts with federal agencies and reports that the administration was considering exempting it from semiconductor tariffs, as listed by congressional Democrats), the President and the White House promoted the film: the White House hosted a screening on January 24, 2026 that TheWrap reports President Trump and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy attended, and the President attended its Kennedy Center premiere. The Pentagon called the film "fantastic" when asked about reports that commanders pressured troops to see it.
government_nexus.note: The First Lady received most of a license fee that the Wall Street Journal reported was nearly three times the next-highest bid, from a company whose founder was rebuilding his relationship with her husband and which had antitrust, contracting, tariff and tax interests before his administration. Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Hank Johnson's letter asks whether the deal was a pay-to-play arrangement; no source shows that any administration decision on Amazon was influenced by the film, and Amazon and Jeff Bezos deny any such purpose. The official promotion (the White House screening, the premiere, the Pentagon's comment) is documented; any link between it and Amazon's regulatory or contracting outcomes is not.

status: Ongoing. The President's 2025 financial disclosure, released June 30, 2026, lists a $10.71 million licensing fee for the film. Amazon and Bezos deny any pay-to-play purpose. A Prime Video docuseries under the same deal was announced for fall 2026, with no premiere date yet.
date_of_action: 2024-12 (Amazon pledges $1 million to the inauguration; Bezos dines with the Trumps at Mar-a-Lago) through 2026-08-04 (the First Lady's adviser announces the follow-up Prime Video docuseries for fall 2026)
what_changed: In December 2024, Amazon announced a $1 million donation to President-elect Trump's inauguration fund and said it would stream the inauguration on Prime Video, a separate in-kind donation worth another $1 million. That month, the Wall Street Journal later reported, Jeff Bezos and his fiancee Lauren Sanchez dined with Donald and Melania Trump at Mar-a-Lago, where Melania, who had consulted director Brett Ratner beforehand, described the documentary she was shopping to studios; Bezos says he "had nothing to do with" the deal and that the Mar-a-Lago account is "not true." On January 5, 2025, Amazon announced that Prime Video had exclusive rights to a documentary about the incoming First Lady, directed by Ratner, with Melania Trump as executive producer. Puck reported, citing three sources, that Amazon paid $40 million. In February 2025, the Wall Street Journal reported that the price was the most Amazon had ever spent on a documentary and nearly three times the next-closest offer (Disney bid $14 million, Paramount $4 million, and Netflix and Apple declined to bid), that the First Lady's cut was more than 70% of the $40 million, and that her agent had separately pitched "sponsorships" starting at $10 million to CEOs and billionaires who attended the inauguration, outreach the Journal said Amazon was unaware of. On March 10, 2025, Prime Video began streaming the first seven seasons of The Apprentice, the show Trump hosted and executive produced; The Hill, citing CNN, said he would likely benefit, though no payment figure has been reported. On January 24, 2026, the First Lady presented "Melania" at a White House screening whose attendees, TheWrap reported, included President Trump, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, Apple CEO Tim Cook and Ratner. The film had its world premiere at the Trump-Kennedy Center on January 29, attended by the President, and opened in theaters January 30 to about $7 million. On January 31, 2026, the Military Religious Freedom Foundation said service members at eight U.S. military facilities had reported being encouraged or pressured by commanders to attend screenings; one anonymous client wrote that a combat-unit commander counted the film toward mandatory unit activity events whose attendance affects fitness evaluations. The Pentagon did not answer whether commanders were encouraging viewings but said, "There is no Department of War directive requiring service members to see this film, though the film is fantastic." The film moved to Prime Video on March 9, 2026, after earning just over $16.4 million domestically. On March 15, 2026, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Hank Johnson, joined by Sen. Ben Ray Lujan and Reps. Dan Goldman and Pramila Jayapal, wrote to Amazon asking whether its $40 million license and reported $35 million marketing budget were part of "a corrupt pay-to-play arrangement," listing Amazon's interests before the administration: the FTC's pending monopolization suit and its settled Prime subscription case, reports that the administration was considering exempting Amazon from semiconductor tariffs, trade-deal lobbying, federal cloud contracts including with immigration agencies, and tax cuts. In a March 30 response, Amazon's vice president of public policy, Brian Huseman, said the company disagreed "with any suggestion that Amazon's decision to license this film and accompanying series was improper" and had followed "a thorough and competitive bidding process"; on April 13, Warren called the response "bribery in plain sight." In mid-May 2026, Ratner flew aboard Air Force One as part of Trump's delegation to Beijing, where his spokeswoman said he would scout locations for "Rush Hour 4," a sequel Trump had privately urged Paramount owner David Ellison to make, Semafor reported in November 2025 (backstory); no source shows a Trump family financial interest in that film. On May 20, 2026, Bezos told CNBC that "the 'Melania' thing is a falsehood that will not die," that the idea it was a way of buying influence is "just not correct," and that the film "appears" to have been "a good business decision," while acknowledging "I can see why people say this." On June 30, 2026, the Office of Government Ethics released the President's 2025 financial disclosure, which listed a $10.71 million licensing fee for "Melania" as 2025 income; White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said, "Neither the President nor his family has ever engaged -- or will ever engage -- in conflicts of interest." On August 4, 2026, the First Lady's senior adviser Marc Beckman announced that a docuseries covered by Amazon's original license would premiere exclusively on Prime Video in the fall.

financial_stake.summary: Amazon paid $40 million to license the film and a follow-up series, the most Amazon had ever spent on a documentary, and reportedly spent another $35 million marketing it; the Wall Street Journal reported more than 70% of the license fee goes to the First Lady, roughly $28 million by lawmakers' estimate; the President's 2025 financial disclosure lists a $10.71 million licensing fee for the film. The film grossed about $16.6 million worldwide.

Box office understates the film's value to Amazon, which also gets streaming rights and the docuseries; Amazon has released no streaming numbers, and Bezos's claim that "it's done very well on streaming" is unverified. Amazon says it licensed the film "for one reason and one reason only -- because we think customers are going to love it," and that the decision "was based on the film and series itself -- the access, the story, and its cultural and historical relevance"; Bezos says he was not involved and the deal was not a way of buying influence. legal_context: Lawful-but-concerning on the public record; no violation has been alleged by any enforcement agency or found. The lawmakers' letter invokes federal anti-bribery law (the federal bribery statute is 18 U.S.C. 201), which bars giving anything of value to a public official, directly or through another person or entity, with intent to influence an official act; a violation requires that corrupt intent and a link to an official act, neither of which any source shows here, and Amazon denies any improper purpose. The main conflict-of-interest statute, 18 U.S.C. 208, which imputes a spouse's financial interests to an official, does not apply to the President (18 U.S.C. 202(c)), so the First Lady's earnings from a company with business before the administration are not themselves covered by it.

The $10.71 million licensing fee is from the President's 2025 financial disclosure as reported by Variety and TheWrap (HIGH); it covers 2025 income only and does not settle the First Lady's full share. The Mar-a-Lago pitch is the Journal's account and is denied by Bezos and, he says, by the First Lady's office. The troop-screening claims come from the Military Religious Freedom Foundation's anonymized clients as relayed to journalist Jonathan Larsen and The Daily Beast; they have not been independently verified, and the Pentagon did not address them directly.
