status: Closed. The CFPB ended its Credova investigation on August 19, 2025. No reopening, court review, inspector general review or congressional inquiry into the closure has been found. Trump Jr. remains a PSQ director, consultant and shareholder.
date_of_action: 2021-02 (CFPB opens its Credova investigation) through 2026-08-13 (Trump Jr. joins a directors' private placement in PSQ stock)
what_changed: Backstory: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau opened an investigation of Credova Financial, a buy now, pay later lender that finances gun purchases, in February 2021, and in August 2024 told the company it was authorized to bring an enforcement action (Bloomberg Law). PublicSquare (PSQ Holdings), a marketplace aimed at conservative-leaning shoppers, had acquired Credova in an all-stock deal in March 2024 (Axios). Donald Trump Jr. had been an investor in PublicSquare since before its IPO, the company said, and on August 9, 2024 he signed a consulting agreement paying him $42,000 a month plus 100,000 restricted stock units. On December 3, 2024, PSQ's board appointed him a director, the same day Omeed Malik resigned from it; Malik is president of 1789 Capital, which Trump Jr. had announced plans to join, and PSQ's stock closed up 270% that day (CNN). According to the CFPB's later account, Bureau staff sent Credova a proposed consent decree that same day, pressed it to settle before the inauguration, and had earlier sought terms requiring it to stop leasing firearms. On August 19, 2025, the CFPB told Credova the investigation was closed. In a letter to PSQ's general counsel, CFPB Chief Legal Officer Mark Paoletta wrote that the probe "exemplifies the type of weaponization against disfavored industries and individuals that President Trump and Acting Director Vought are committed to ending," that it "was not aimed at protecting consumers, but at suppressing activities protected by the First and Second Amendment," and that the settlement demands "unmistakably appear targeted at shutting down Credova's firearms business"; he cited the President's executive order on debanking and noted that the proposed consent decree arrived the day PSQ announced Trump Jr.'s board seat. PSQ's CEO thanked "President Trump, Acting Director Vought, CFPB Chief Legal Officer Mark Paoletta, CFPB Senior Adviser Jeff Clark, and the CFPB staff." AP reported Credova's record: a 2021 Massachusetts settlement waiving more than $126,000 in balances over allegedly illegal dog leases, a January 2024 California consent order with a $50,000 penalty over undisclosed third-party fees, and more than 50 complaints in the CFPB's database. CREW's January 2026 roundup of companies that added Trump Jr. to their boards listed the closure and noted that Credova finances purchases at GrabAGun, the Trump Jr.-backed gun retailer. In a CFPB semi-annual report described by Consumer Finance Monitor in January 2026, Vought wrote that Credova's financing of Second Amendment purchases "made it a target for the Bureau" and that "Under my leadership, that investigation was closed." Paoletta became the CFPB's Acting Director on August 1, 2026. PSQ's 2026 proxy shows Trump Jr. earned $504,000 in consulting fees for 2025 and held 797,403 shares, and on August 13, 2026 he was among six directors who bought $1.3 million of new PSQ stock in a private placement.

financial_stake.summary: Trump Jr. is paid by PSQ as a director and as a consultant ($42,000 a month) and held about 1.6% of its stock in its 2026 proxy. Credova is part of PSQ's financial technology business; closing the case ended the prospect of the penalties and firearms-leasing limits that, by the CFPB's account, Biden-era staff had sought.

The SEC's closure of the Crypto.com probe came under Acting Chair Mark Uyeda, before Paul Atkins took office, during a five-week wave in which the SEC dropped investigations and suits against Coinbase, Consensys, Robinhood, Gemini, Uniswap, OpenSea and others; the OCC granted similar conditional charters to Circle, Ripple, Paxos and Bridge. What the record does show is a company under SEC investigation becoming a business partner of the President's company, giving $35 million to his super PAC, and winning favorable decisions from agencies in his administration. Sen. Warren told the SEC that a sitting president asking an agency in his administration to approve products from a company he controls was, quoting the Wall Street Journal, "without precedent."

status: Ended: Yorkville withdrew all three Truth Social crypto ETF registrations on May 19, 2026 with no shares sold, and on Aug. 7, 2026 the partners ended the CRO treasury SPAC and Crypto.com's ETF servicing role. Truth Social stock ETFs still trade. No agency has found wrongdoing.
date_of_action: 2025-03-24 (Trump Media and Crypto.com announce a crypto ETF partnership) through 2026-08-07 (Trump Media, Crypto.com and Yorkville terminate the CRO treasury deal and ETF servicing partnership)
what_changed:
Backstory: the SEC sent Crypto.com a Wells notice in August 2024 signaling it planned to take legal action, and Crypto.com sued the agency in October. The Associated Press reported that SEC commissioners under President Biden had authorized charges, but that the company's lawyers negotiated to delay any enforcement action until after Trump took office, and in exchange Crypto.com withdrew its suit; the AP notes such negotiations are common before the SEC brings a case. The suit was dropped after CEO Kris Marszalek met President-elect Trump at Mar-a-Lago on December 16, 2024, with a spokesperson saying the company looked forward "to working with the new administration." Crypto.com gave $1 million to Trump's inauguration that December and $10 million to his super PAC, MAGA Inc., in February 2025, and stepped up lobbying payments to Jeff Miller, a Trump fundraiser who lobbied the White House and the SEC, according to the AP.

On March 24, 2025, Trump Media & Technology Group and Crypto.com announced a partnership to launch "Made in America" exchange-traded funds under Trump Media's Truth.Fi brand, with Crypto.com supplying infrastructure and custody for a possible basket of tokens including bitcoin, ether and Crypto.com's own Cronos (CRO). Three days later, on March 27, Crypto.com said the SEC had closed its investigation with no action. The SEC was then led by Acting Chairman Mark Uyeda; Trump's nominee, Paul Atkins, had not yet taken office, and the closure followed five weeks in which the SEC dropped cases or probes involving Coinbase, Robinhood, Uniswap and other crypto firms. On April 22 Trump Media said it had signed a binding agreement with Crypto.com and Yorkville America Digital. On April 25, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, wrote to SEC Chairman Atkins calling the plan "an extraordinary conflict of interest" and asking him by May 2 to preserve all SEC records on the deal, list any communications with the White House about Trump Media, and say how the agency would keep its decisions free of political influence. No response from the SEC has been found.

NYSE Arca filed on June 3, 2025 to list the Truth Social Bitcoin ETF, and registration statements for it, a Truth Social Bitcoin & Ethereum ETF and a Truth Social Crypto Blue Chip ETF were filed between June and July 2025, with Yorkville America as sponsor. The SEC later pushed back its decision on the Bitcoin & Ethereum fund by 45 days, to October 8, 2025, alongside identical delays for other issuers' crypto ETFs while new exchange listing standards were pending. On August 26, 2025, Trump Media, Crypto.com and the blank-check company Yorkville Acquisition Corp. announced Trump Media Group CRO Strategy, a planned Nasdaq-listed company (ticker MCGA) to hold CRO, targeting at least $6.42 billion: about $1 billion in CRO from Crypto.com, $200 million in cash, $220 million in warrants and a $5 billion credit line from a Yorkville affiliate. Trump Media separately bought about 684 million CRO, worth about $105 million, from a Crypto.com affiliate, paying $50 million in cash and 2,797,985 of its own shares, according to its Form 8-K. The AP reported that Crypto.com was to contribute most of the capital while Trump Media's contribution included "a license to use certain intellectual property." In October 2025 Trump Media announced Truth Predict, a Crypto.com-powered prediction market for Truth Social users, and Yorkville Acquisition later confidentially filed its merger registration with the SEC, expecting to close in the first quarter of 2026.

In February 2026, FEC filings showed Crypto.com's parent, Foris DAX, had given MAGA Inc. another $5 million in January, bringing its total to $35 million in about a year, including $10 million in October 2025, the month it applied to the OCC for a trust bank charter. That month the CFTC, led by Chairman Mike Selig, filed a motion supporting Crypto.com in its lawsuit against Nevada over sports prediction markets, months after Selig told a Senate committee he would defer to the courts on the issue, and, American Banker reported on February 24, the OCC conditionally approved a national trust bank charter for Foris DAX, to do business as Crypto.com National Trust Bank.

The ventures then came apart. On May 19, 2026, Yorkville withdrew all three Truth Social crypto ETF registrations, stating that none had been declared effective and "no securities have been sold," and said it would shift to funds under the Investment Company Act of 1940; Bloomberg Intelligence analyst James Seyffart pointed to competition from cheaper bitcoin ETFs as the more likely reason. On August 7, 2026, Crypto.com, Trump Media and Yorkville Acquisition announced they would mutually terminate the CRO Strategy business combination before it closed, "citing prevailing market conditions, and shifting business and stakeholder priorities," and would drop the plan for Crypto.com to service Yorkville America's planned ETFs. Interim Trump Media CEO Kevin McGurn told Axios the digital-asset treasury market had grown crowded; Truth Predict was scaled back to a marketing deal promoting Crypto.com's prediction markets to Truth Social users, and CRO traded at about $0.05. Yorkville's existing Truth Social stock ETFs continue.

financial_stake.summary: The CRO treasury was pitched at $6.42 billion, built mostly on Crypto.com's CRO, with Trump Media's share still undisclosed in December 2025; it was terminated before closing. Trump Media bought about $105 million of CRO from a Crypto.com affiliate, paying $50 million in cash and 2,797,985 of its own shares. Trump Media licenses the Truth Social name to Yorkville's stock ETFs, which held about $150 million, for an undisclosed fee; the crypto ETFs never sold a share.

financial_stake.caveat: There is no public figure for what Yorkville pays Trump Media to license the Truth Social name; the New York Times found only "an unspecified amount" in filings, and Trump Media and Yorkville declined to discuss it. Trump Media's stake in the CRO treasury was never disclosed, and whether it still holds its CRO is not confirmed. Trump gains through his shareholding, not direct payments. Crypto.com said the SEC probe "was closed because there was no legitimate case to pursue" and "There is absolutely no connection between that decision and Crypto.com's" political activities, that its lobbyist Jeff Miller "had no involvement" with the SEC investigation, and that it partners with companies that are "pro crypto." Trump Media called the AP's story "obviously spoon-fed" by "political operatives" and said Warren was "harassing and intimidating America-First companies." CFTC Chairman Mike Selig said the agency "will no longer sit idly by while overzealous state governments undermine the agency's exclusive jurisdiction over these markets." The White House says neither Trump nor his family has "ever engaged, or will ever engage, in conflicts of interest."

legal_context: Lawful-but-concerning: no agency, court or ethics office has found wrongdoing. The crypto ETFs needed SEC action on an exchange listing filing (Form 19b-4) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and on registration statements under the Securities Act of 1933; Yorkville withdrew them under SEC Rule 477 and said it would use the Investment Company Act of 1940 instead. The OCC's national trust charters let crypto firms conduct non-fiduciary activities such as custody under its 2021 Interpretive Letter 1176, written by Jonathan Gould when he was the agency's general counsel.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the deal terms and dates, which rest on the companies' joint August 7, 2026 release filed with the SEC, Trump Media's August 26, 2025 Form 8-K, Sen. Warren's letter, Yorkville's withdrawal language as quoted by BeInCrypto, and consistent trade-press accounts (Cointelegraph, CryptoSlate, Decrypt). The account of Crypto.com's negotiations with the SEC, its donations and lobbying, and the companies' responses rests on the Associated Press. The OCC approval date rests on American Banker and Crypto.com's announcement, not the OCC's own letter; the CFTC filing rests on Decrypt and American Banker, not the court filing itself. Every connection between the partnership and an agency act is timing only: the SEC closed many crypto cases in the same weeks, and the OCC gave other crypto firms similar charters. There is no public figure for Trump Media's licensing income from the Truth Social funds, and the SEC's final handling of the crypto ETFs' exchange filings is not confirmed.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Trump Media turned to financial products as its social platform struggled to make money, and Crypto.com became its main partner. The pattern this entry records is a company under SEC investigation that became the President's business partner and a large donor to his super PAC, and then received favorable decisions from the SEC, the OCC and the CFTC. Each decision has an innocent explanation in the record: the SEC was dropping crypto cases across the industry, the OCC was chartering many crypto firms, and the CFTC said it was defending its exclusive jurisdiction over prediction markets. The partnership never produced the crypto ETFs or the $6.42 billion CRO treasury. The same family-business-meets-regulator pattern runs through the World Liberty entry, where the bank regulator granted the family venture's trust bank a preliminary charter, and the Truth API entry, which concerns another Trump Media product.
pull_quote: "When you consider the investigation into (Crypto.com) was dropped, the economics of this look more like a plea deal than a business deal." -- Corey Frayer, a former senior SEC official, to the AP

title: Trump appointees held stock in the President's Trump Media: share awards to nominees Patel and McMahon, Bondi's sale on tariff day, and a Swiss central bank stake

business_entity.name: Trump Media & Technology Group
business_entity.family_stake: President Trump owned around 53% of Trump Media (Nasdaq: DJT) in early 2025, according to CREW, a stake Politico valued at about $3.6 billion. Weeks after the 2024 election he moved it into his revocable trust, of which he is the sole beneficiary and Donald Trump Jr. the only trustee, CNBC reported. Trump Jr. also sits on Trump Media's board and received the same 25,946-share award in January 2025 as fellow directors Kash Patel and Linda McMahon.

government_nexus.action: Three people tied to Trump Media stock took top posts in the President's administration. Trump Media awarded 25,946 shares each to directors Kash Patel and Linda McMahon while their nominations for FBI Director and Education Secretary were pending; Patel's award was not on his financial disclosure report. Attorney General Pam Bondi sold her Trump Media shares and warrants on April 2, 2025, the day the President announced his 'Liberation Day' tariffs after the market closed.

official.name: Kash Patel
official.role: Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation (confirmed Feb. 20, 2025; Trump Media director until then)

also_officials.name: Linda McMahon
also_officials.role: Secretary of Education (Trump Media director while nominated)

government_nexus.note: The conflict is ownership, not a contract or ruling: officials who lead the FBI and the Justice Department, which investigate securities fraud and public corruption, and the Education Department either held or were awarded stock of a company majority-owned by the President who appointed them. Patel declined his award and McMahon forfeited future equity on leaving the board, and Bondi was selling under a divestiture deadline in her ethics agreement. No source shows Bondi had advance, nonpublic knowledge of the tariff announcement. The Swiss National Bank purchase involves no U.S. official act; it is included because CREW described it as the first known foreign government-connected investment in the President's public company.

status: No finding: no agency has found wrongdoing in Bondi's April 2, 2025 sale; Rep. Raskin's May 2025 request for a DOJ inspector general probe has no public result, and Bondi left office in April 2026. Trump Media's 2025 proxy lists no award for Patel and says McMahon forfeited future equity.
date_of_action: 2024-07 (Swiss National Bank's third-quarter 2024 purchase of Trump Media shares begins) through 2026-04-02 (Trump announces Bondi is out as Attorney General)
what_changed:
In the third quarter of 2024, the Swiss National Bank, Switzerland's central bank, about half of whose share capital is held by cantons, cantonal banks and other public bodies, bought 111,300 shares of Trump Media & Technology Group worth $1.78 million, according to an SEC filing from November 2024 obtained by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW). The Zürcher Kantonalbank, owned by the canton of Zurich, held 14,796 shares worth $237,000. CREW called it "the first known apparent instance of a foreign government-connected entity being invested in the president's public company," while noting the banks may have sold shares not yet reported. In December 2024, President-elect Trump moved his majority Trump Media stake into a revocable trust controlled by Donald Trump Jr.

On January 17, 2025, Pam Bondi's ethics agreement as attorney general nominee was posted. Her financial disclosure showed she had been paid in shares of Digital World Acquisition Corp., the blank-check company that merged with Trump Media, worth more than $2.9 million, for consulting for Renatus LLC, a firm run by Trump Media director Eric Swider. She pledged to "divest my interests in Trump Media & Technology Group, as soon as practicable but not later than 90 days after my confirmation" and to stay out of matters affecting it until then.

On January 28, 2025, Trump Media granted 25,946 restricted stock units each to its six directors, among them FBI Director nominee Kash Patel, Education Secretary nominee Linda McMahon and Donald Trump Jr., "as consideration for services provided" in 2024. At that day's close they were worth about $779,400 apiece; a quarter vested at once and the rest vests quarterly through March 2027. The filings became public on January 30, hours after Patel's Senate confirmation hearing. In a Senate questionnaire dated that day, Patel wrote that "out of an abundance of caution and to avoid any appearance of any conflict, I did not and will not accept that compensation." Business Insider reported on February 7 that the award was not on Patel's financial disclosure report. McMahon said in disclosures published by the Office of Government Ethics on February 7 that she planned to forfeit most of her stock if confirmed and divest the rest within 90 days of confirmation.

On February 10, 2025, the Swiss National Bank filed a disclosure showing it held 157,500 Trump Media shares, valued at $5.37 million, at the end of 2024, up from its third-quarter position. The Senate confirmed Patel as FBI Director on February 20, and he stepped down from Trump Media's board that day; former Interior Secretary David Bernhardt replaced him.

On March 18, 2025, Trump Media's proxy statement listed no stock award or other pay for Patel, noting he "will not be accepting any compensation for his Board service," while still listing McMahon's 25,946 units, valued at $779,418 when granted. It said Patel and McMahon "resigned from their positions on the Board in 2025 and, upon resigning, forfeited future cash and equity compensation."

On April 1, 2025, Trump Media filed an SEC disclosure listing holdings of top shareholders, including Trump and Bondi, that appeared to re-register their shares for sale. On April 2, Bondi sold between $1 million and $5 million of Trump Media shares and between $250,000 and $500,000 of Trump Media warrants, according to her disclosure forms, which ProPublica reported on May 14. President Trump's "Liberation Day" tariff announcement came after the market closed that day. The forms do not say whether her sales came before or after the close, or at what price. Trump Media closed at $18.76 on April 2, opened at $17.92 the next morning and fell 13% over the following days before rebounding; NOTUS put the low at $16.66 on April 8. The sale fell within her ethics agreement's 90-day deadline, which ran to early May.

On May 20, 2025, Rep. Jamie Raskin, ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, asked Justice Department Inspector General Michael Horowitz to investigate whether Bondi or other DOJ officials engaged in illegal insider trading ahead of the tariff announcement, writing that her sale "appears to have saved her, at the very least, hundreds of thousands of dollars." The Justice Department did not respond to ProPublica or NOTUS. No public response from the inspector general has been found.

On April 2, 2026, President Trump announced that Bondi was out as attorney general, with Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche as acting attorney general; NPR reported that her departure followed frustration over her leadership and her handling of the Epstein files; its report does not mention the stock sale.

financial_stake.summary: Each Trump Media director, including Patel, McMahon and Trump Jr., was awarded 25,946 shares worth about $779,400 to $826,000 in early 2025; the company later said Patel took no award and McMahon forfeited future equity. Bondi sold $1 million to $5 million of Trump Media shares and $250,000 to $500,000 of warrants on April 2, 2025, from stock she was paid for consulting. The Swiss National Bank held 157,500 Trump Media shares worth $5.37 million at the end of 2024. The President's own stake was worth about $3.6 billion.

financial_stake.caveat: Bondi's figures are the broad ranges federal disclosure forms use, not exact amounts, and the forms give no time or price for her sales, so how much she gained or avoided losing is unknown; Rep. Raskin's estimate that she saved "at the very least, hundreds of thousands of dollars" is his own. The award values are paper values at stated closing prices; most of each award was restricted. Trump Media's March 2025 proxy statement lists no stock award for Patel and says he and McMahon "upon resigning, forfeited future cash and equity compensation"; it still lists McMahon's 25,946-unit grant, and no filing found shows what became of the quarter that vested at once. The Swiss National Bank's SEC filings show it kept the stake, holding 319,300 shares worth about $2.47 million on June 30, 2026, among 2,301 U.S. stock positions. Patel said he "did not and will not accept" the award to avoid "any appearance of any conflict," McMahon pledged to forfeit most of hers and divest the rest, and Bondi's sale was required by her ethics agreement within 90 days of confirmation. The Justice Department did not respond to questions about the sale, and Trump Media and the White House did not immediately comment on the awards. ProPublica noted that it is unclear whether Bondi knew any nonpublic details of the tariffs, which Trump had promised since the campaign.

legal_context: Lawful-but-concerning as far as any finding goes: no agency, court or ethics office has found a violation. Bondi's divestiture pledge and recusal language track the federal conflict-of-interest statute, 18 U.S.C. § 208, and nominees' financial disclosure reports are required by the Ethics in Government Act of 1978. Trading on material nonpublic information learned through government work can violate the insider-trading ban of section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934; the STOCK Act of 2012 affirms that executive branch employees are not exempt from it, though, as ProPublica notes, such cases against officials are legally difficult. CREW argues that foreign government-connected purchases of Trump Media stock raise questions under the Constitution's Emoluments Clauses; no court has ruled on that question.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the share awards, which rest on Trump Media's SEC filings as reported consistently by CNBC, Politico and Business Insider, and on Patel's own questionnaire answer. Bondi's sales rest on her disclosure forms as reported by ProPublica and NOTUS, which give only dollar ranges and no time of day. Whether Bondi had any advance, nonpublic knowledge of the tariff announcement is the disputed point: Rep. Raskin says the sale "bears all the hallmarks of insider trading," but no evidence of such knowledge has been published and no investigation has been confirmed. The Swiss National Bank figures rest on CREW's reading of the bank's SEC filings and were confirmed against the bank's 13F reports, which also show the later quarters. Trump Media's March 18, 2025 proxy statement records that Patel took no award and that he and McMahon forfeited future cash and equity compensation on leaving its board; no filing shows the disposition of McMahon's immediately vested units.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Trump Media is a publicly traded company majority-owned by the President, so anyone who owns its shares has a financial stake in his political fortunes, and anyone can buy in. This entry records three ways that played out early in his second term: the company paid its directors in stock while two of them were awaiting confirmation to run the FBI and the Education Department, the Attorney General who held its shares sold them on the day of a market-moving presidential announcement, and a foreign central bank became a shareholder. Each has an innocent explanation in the record: the awards were routine director pay that the nominees said they would give up, Bondi had to sell by early May anyway, and a central bank's stake can reflect a broad stock portfolio rather than a political choice. The same company's dealings with federal regulators are covered in the Trump Media and Crypto.com entry, and the President's own trading in the stock-trading entry.
pull_quote: "This conduct bears all the hallmarks of insider trading and demands impartial investigation." -- Rep. Jamie Raskin, letter to the Justice Department inspector general on Attorney General Bondi's Trump Media sale (May 20, 2025)

title: Trump's $TRUMP meme coin, which earned his company $635M, rewarded top buyers with dinners with the President and a White House tour

business_entity.name: $TRUMP
business_entity.family_stake: The coin is run by a Trump Organization affiliate, CIC Digital LLC, and Fight Fight Fight LLC, a Delaware company led by Trump friend Bill Zanker; together they own 80 percent of the coins, the Washington Post reported, and both collect a portion of the fees on $TRUMP trades, CREW found. Trump's financial disclosure released in mid-2026 lists $636 million in earnings from CIC Digital, most of it from a $635 million licensing agreement with Celebration Coin for the sale of the $TRUMP meme coin, ABC News reported. Trump told CNBC in 2026 that his son Eric "handles" the money, CNN reported.

government_nexus.action: The President's personal appearances at events open only to the coin's top holders: a May 22, 2025 dinner for the top 220 holders at his Virginia golf club, with a VIP reception for the top 25 and a White House tour for top investors the next day; an April 25, 2026 Mar-a-Lago luncheon for the top 297; and a third gala for the top 185 advertised for November 2026.
government_nexus.note: The access is offered in exchange for buying and holding a coin that pays Trump-affiliated entities: CIC Digital and Fight Fight Fight earn fees on trades, and the first dinner announcement set off a buying surge. Buyers included foreign holders and parties with business before the government: the self-described top holder, Tron founder Justin Sun, faced a 2023 SEC civil fraud case that the SEC moved to pause in February 2025 and settled in March 2026 with every claim against Sun dismissed; Freight Technologies said its purchase was a way "to advocate for fair, balanced, and free trade between Mexico and the US." China-linked GD Culture Group, which sells through TikTok, announced a $TRUMP buying plan while Trump was seeking a TikTok deal; no report shows it bought. The White House says the events are private and that Trump attends on his own time.

status: A third $TRUMP holders' gala with Trump is set for Nov. 22, 2026; CBS News found over half of the top 100 contenders used exchanges closed to Americans. No OGE or SEC action on senators' 2025 and 2026 requests has been reported. The coin trades about 97% below its January 2025 peak.
date_of_action: 2025-01-17 (Trump announces the $TRUMP meme coin) through 2026-10-14 (CBS News analysis of the third gala's leaderboard)
what_changed:
On January 17, 2025, three days before his inauguration, Trump announced $TRUMP, a meme coin; first lady Melania Trump's $MELANIA coin was announced two days later. The coin, which has no attached asset or underlying value, spiked to a $15 billion market cap right after launch before crashing within days, CNBC reported. Eighty percent of the coins are owned by CIC Digital, a Trump Organization affiliate, and Fight Fight Fight, a company led by Trump friend Bill Zanker. Asked that week whether he would keep selling products that benefit him personally, Trump said "I don't know if it benefited" and "I don't know much about it, other than I launched it." By February 9, 2025, Chainalysis data showed nearly $100 million in trading fees had flowed to the family and its partners while more than 810,000 wallets had lost money, more than $2 billion in all; one unidentified wallet that bought less than two minutes after Trump's announcement made as much as $109 million in two days, the New York Times reported, adding that no evidence had emerged that Trump or his associates inflated the price or traded on inside information. In February 2025 the SEC moved to pause its 2023 civil fraud case against Tron founder Justin Sun, about a month after Sun's $75 million investment in the Trump family's World Liberty Financial token, ABC News reported. On February 27, 2025, the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance said meme coins are "akin to collectibles" and that transactions in them "do not involve the offer and sale of securities," so "neither meme coin purchasers nor holders are protected by the federal securities laws."

On April 23, 2025, the coin's website announced that its top 220 holders would be invited to an "intimate private dinner" with the President on May 22 at Trump National Golf Club outside Washington, and that the top 25 would get a private VIP reception with him and "a Special White House Tour." **Within an hour the coin's price had surged almost 60 percent.** A Washington Post analysis found 27 wallets had each bought more than 100,000 coins after the announcement, the largest about $24 million worth, and estimated that the coin had earned Trump and his partners about $41 million in fees and $312 million in sales since launch; Chainalysis put fees routed to the project's wallets at about $324.5 million. On April 25, 2025, Sens. Adam Schiff and Elizabeth Warren asked the Office of Government Ethics for an urgent inquiry, writing that the offer may implicate "the federal bribery statute and emoluments clauses of the U.S. Constitution." On April 30 Freight Technologies, a Nasdaq-listed U.S.-Mexico freight firm, announced plans to buy up to $20 million of $TRUMP; its CEO called the tokens "an effective way to advocate for fair, balanced, and free trade between Mexico and the US." On May 12 GD Culture Group, a Nasdaq-listed firm with a Chinese subsidiary, eight employees and no revenue the previous year, said it would buy up to $300 million of Bitcoin and $TRUMP with proceeds from a stock sale to an unnamed British Virgin Islands entity, and confirmed the plan in an SEC filing the next day; the New York Times said any purchase would be the first known by a China-linked firm and that it was unclear whether the company would follow through. The contest closed on May 12. The top wallet, under the name "Sun," held about 1.43 million coins worth over $19 million, WIRED reported, and a Bloomberg analysis found 19 of the top 25 wallets almost certainly belonged to people operating outside the U.S. Freight Technologies spent $2 million and finished 250th, missing the cut. Within days of qualifying, about 100 of the 220 winners, including 17 of the 25 VIPs, had sold or moved nearly all their coins, WIRED found.

The dinner went ahead on May 22, 2025. The contest drew an estimated $148 million in purchases, according to Inca Digital, and Justin Sun said he was the top-ranked investor. Press secretary Karoline Leavitt said that day that "the president is attending [the dinner] in his personal time. It is not a White House dinner." Two attendees told the New York Times, as The New Republic reported, what they expected: Vincent Liu of Taiwan-based Kronos Research said he would "definitely not hesitate to share my perspective," and Korean crypto executive Sangrok Oh called it "kind of a fund-raiser" for Trump: "he'll always be good to his sponsors." White House officials told CBS News they had not approved the initial plan for a White House tour. On May 23 several top investors visited the White House for what they described as a special VIP event, ABC News reported, and Sun posted a video of his tour: "Was an honor to be invited to tour the @WhiteHouse." Sens. Richard Blumenthal, Chris Murphy, Warren and Jeff Merkley and Rep. Sam Liccardo asked in May 2025 who attended and what they expected in return; no attendee list was made public.

On March 5, 2026, the SEC filed a settlement of its case against Sun, which the court entered as a final judgment on March 9: every claim against Sun personally, the Tron Foundation and the BitTorrent Foundation was dismissed with prejudice, and the BitTorrent developer Rainberry agreed to a $10 million penalty, with no admission of wrongdoing. On March 12, 2026, the coin's website began promoting the April 25 Mar-a-Lago event, organized by Fight Fight Fight, and the coin briefly rose to $3.08, Politico reported. On April 9, 2026, Sens. Warren, Schiff and Blumenthal asked Fight Fight Fight for documents on the President's role in planning, promoting and profiting from the April 25 Mar-a-Lago event. On April 25, 2026, the top 297 holders were invited to a Mar-a-Lago luncheon where Trump spoke, and he met separately with the top 29. Trump's financial disclosure for 2025, released at the end of June 2026, listed $636 million in earnings from CIC Digital, most of it from a $635 million licensing agreement with Celebration Coin for the sale of the coin. On August 3, 2026, Warren and Blumenthal asked SEC Chair Paul Atkins to investigate, writing that "President Trump's memecoin scheme may constitute an illegal scam"; by then almost 1 million people had lost a total of $3.8 billion on the coin through the end of June, according to Nansen research reported by the New York Times and cited by CNN. **At the start of October 2026 the coin's website advertised a third gala with the President at the same Virginia club for the top 185 holders, with a VIP reception for the top 29 and an 18-karat Trump-branded gold watch for the top four, the contest running through November 12;** the coin then traded at $2.06, 97 percent below its $75.35 peak of January 19, 2025, Forbes reported. On October 14, 2026, a CBS News analysis found that at least 52 of the top 100 holders competing for seats had moved money through crypto exchanges that bar U.S. customers.

financial_stake.summary: Trump's 2025 disclosure shows $635 million from a licensing agreement for $TRUMP sales, through CIC Digital, a Trump Organization affiliate that with Fight Fight Fight owns 80% of the coins. The first dinner contest drew an estimated $148 million in buying; nearly a million buyers had lost about $3.8 billion by mid-2026.

financial_stake.caveat: The $635 million is ABC News's reading of Trump's disclosure; the fee, purchase and loss figures are blockchain-analytics estimates built from pseudonymous wallets, and Chainalysis stopped tracking the coin in May 2025. How much of the coin's revenue reaches Trump personally rather than Fight Fight Fight's other partners is not public. The White House's case: the first dinner was "a personal dinner that the president is attending on his personal time" and "the White House has absolutely nothing to do with it"; for the 2026 gala a White House official said organizers promised no private meet-and-greet and "there is no promise of official government action in exchange for attending," and the White House says Trump's portfolio is managed by third-party financial institutions. Trump says he followed the law and his son Eric handles his finances. The coin's website says $TRUMP is "not political." Sun and his companies settled the SEC case without admitting or denying its allegations, and no source ties the SEC's handling of it to his $TRUMP purchases.

legal_context: Lawful-but-concerning conduct as reported; no violation has been found and no one has been charged. The federal conflict-of-interest law does not apply to the president, CNN noted, and CREW's spokesman said no law applying to the president would be violated "unless one of the top 25 holders was something like a foreign state's wealth fund," which could bring in the Foreign Emoluments Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, sec. 9, cl. 8); no foreign-government buyer has been identified. Sens. Schiff and Warren said the offer may implicate the federal bribery statute (18 U.S.C. 201), which turns on proof of an exchange for an official act; no investigation has been reported. In February 2025 SEC staff said meme coins generally are not securities but that products labeled meme coins to evade the securities laws are judged case by case; Sens. Warren and Blumenthal have asked the SEC to examine $TRUMP on that basis.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the dinner offer, its terms and dates, the May 22, 2025 dinner and the May 23 White House visit, from the coin's own announcement as quoted by Mother Jones and WIRED, and from CNBC, ABC News and CBS News. HIGH confidence on the $635 million disclosure line, reported by ABC News and repeated by CNN. MODERATE confidence on fee, purchase, foreign-holder and loss figures: they are estimates by blockchain-analytics firms (Chainalysis, Inca Digital, Bloomberg's analysis, Nansen, Arkham) working from pseudonymous wallets, and outlets' fee totals differ. Justin Sun publicly said he was the top holder. TAP found no public response from the Office of Government Ethics to the April 2025 letter or from Fight Fight Fight to the April 2026 letter, no SEC action on the August 2026 letter, and no published attendee list. TAP found no report that GD Culture Group completed its announced $TRUMP purchase. The Times's early-trader figures come from Chainalysis, Nansen and an independent researcher, and the Times reported no evidence of insider trading. A New York Times report on a Chinese political-advisory-body member attending the 2025 dinner could not be read and is left out. Disputed: critics and Democratic senators call the dinners pay-to-play sales of presidential access; the White House says they are private events with no promise of official action.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of the Trump family's wider crypto business that federal crypto policy touches: the self-described top $TRUMP buyer, Justin Sun, was also an early World Liberty Financial backer, and the same industry's clemency and enforcement side appears in the crypto-pardon entry and the DOJ crypto-enforcement entry.
pull_quote: CREW's Jordan Libowitz: ‘This is about as unethical as you can get—essentially selling off access to the president and the White House.’

glance.what: Spoke at dinners for top buyers of his $TRUMP coin, which paid his company $635M; some toured the White House

title: Trump Mobile marketed a "made in the USA" phone that shipped as a reskinned HTC while the President's appointees at the FCC and FTC oversaw it

business_entity.name: Trump Mobile
business_entity.family_stake: Trump Mobile is run by T1 Mobile LLC, a separate company that licenses the Trump name (Washington Post). The President's 2026 annual financial disclosure lists the licensor, DT Marks Mobile LLC (licensee: T1 Mobile LLC), as owned 79% by DTTM Operations LLC, 20% by "Trump Family Members" and 1% by its managing-member corporation. Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. unveiled the venture and introduced its launch team; who owns T1 Mobile LLC itself is not public.

government_nexus.action: The FCC, which regulates mobile virtual network operators like Trump Mobile, certified in January 2026 a phone that FCC records reviewed by The Verge appear to show is the T1 (the applicant was Smart Gadgets Global, whose CEO is Trump Mobile executive Eric Thomas), after FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in June 2025 he had no discussions with the White House about the venture and would "run our normal process." The FTC, which enforces "Made in USA" and delivery rules, has taken no public action after lawmakers in August 2025 and January 2026 asked it to explain how it would police Trump Mobile.
government_nexus.note: The link is regulatory oversight, not a contract, grant or policy decision for the venture. Agencies led by the President's appointees regulate the network, certify the device and enforce the marketing rules for a business licensing his name, and lawmakers asked how they would avoid favoring it. The one documented official act, the FCC device certification, is a routine equipment approval; no source shows it or any other agency decision was influenced by the Trump connection. House Democrats also questioned whether T-Mobile, whose network carries the service and which won two FCC deal approvals in July 2025 after ending its DEI programs, was positioned to gain regulatory favor; no source links those approvals to Trump Mobile. In October 2026 Sen. Maggie Hassan said Trump Mobile appeared to lack a required FCC robocall-mitigation filing and international-calling authorization; no FCC enforcement action has been announced.

status: Ongoing. Trump Mobile began shipping the T1 in May 2026, nine months late; a June 2026 teardown found it a near-copy of the HTC U24 Pro. No FTC action has been found; an Oct. 8, 2026 letter from Sen. Maggie Hassan says it appears to lack FCC robocall filings and international-calling authorization.
date_of_action: 2025-06-16 (Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. unveil Trump Mobile) through October 8, 2026 (Sen. Maggie Hassan asks Trump Mobile about missing FCC filings and the reported customer-data theft)
what_changed: On June 16, 2025, Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. unveiled Trump Mobile at Trump Tower, a $47.45-a-month wireless service and a gold $499 T1 smartphone, run by a separate company, T1 Mobile, that licenses the Trump brand; Eric Trump said the phones would "eventually all … be built in the United States," while the website said "MADE IN THE USA." The White House said: "President Trump's assets are in a trust managed by his children. There are no conflicts of interest." That night, the company deleted its coverage map after users noticed it labeled the "Gulf of Mexico," not the "Gulf of America" of Trump's executive order. On June 17, analysts told CNBC the T1 would likely be produced by a Chinese original device manufacturer; IDC's Francisco Jeronimo said U.S. manufacture was "completely impossible." By about June 25, the website had dropped its made-in-USA language for phrases such as "designed with American values in mind." On June 26, FCC Chair Brendan Carr told reporters he had no discussions with the White House about Trump Mobile, learned of it from a press release, and would "run our normal process if there's anything that needs to be done by the FCC." On July 10, 404 Media reporter Joseph Cox wrote that Trump Mobile had charged his card again for a phone he had not received, after a pre-order that charged the wrong amount. On July 23, House Energy and Commerce Democrats Frank Pallone, Doris Matsui and Yvette Clarke wrote to T-Mobile's CEO that its role in carrying the service through Liberty Mobile Wireless, while Trump is President and appoints the FCC chair, "presents a conflict of interest," asking about any contacts with the White House or the Trump Organization by August 6; Reuters noted that earlier that month the FCC had approved two T-Mobile deals after the carrier ended its DEI programs. On July 31, Reuters reported that Liberty Mobile is co-owned by launch-team members Pat O'Brien, Eric Thomas and Don Hendrickson, that the bundled roadside, device-protection and health-tracking services come from companies tied to them, and that a spokesperson said the T1 was being made in Alabama, California and Florida. On August 5, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and five other Democrats asked the FCC, FTC, FDA, Commerce, Treasury and the Trade Representative how they would avoid favoring the venture. The phone missed its August and October targets; on December 31, Fortune reported that customer service blamed the government shutdown, saying "They had to pause everything on the FCC side of things." In January 2026 the FCC certified a phone from Smart Gadgets Global, whose CEO is Trump Mobile executive Eric Thomas. On January 15, 2026, eleven Democrats led by Warren asked FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson whether the FTC had opened an investigation into the made-in-USA claims and the $100 deposits for undelivered phones, noting it never answered their August letter; no public reply has been found. Before shipping began, the company changed its terms to say the $100 deposit is only a "conditional opportunity" to buy the phone. On May 13, 2026, CEO Pat O'Brien said pre-ordered phones were being delivered and that the first devices are "assembled in the U.S." In June 2026, an iFixit teardown of a unit NBC News obtained found the T1 nearly identical to the HTC U24 Pro, a phone Taiwan's regulator lists as made by a China-based manufacturer; TechSpot reported the T1's final assembly is in Miami. On June 30, 2026, the President's annual disclosure listed the licensor, DT Marks Mobile LLC, with income of less than $201 for 2025. By early October 2026, a hacking group, BYOD, claimed to have stolen data on 3,615 customers through a Liberty Mobile employee. On October 8, 2026, Sen. Maggie Hassan wrote to CEO Pat O'Brien that searches found no FCC Robocall Mitigation Database filing under Trump Mobile or T1 Mobile LLC and no authorization she says it needs for its advertised international calling, and asked whether it had told the FCC, the FBI and customers about the breach, with answers due October 29. No FCC enforcement action has been announced.

financial_stake.summary: The terms of the Trump name license are undisclosed, and the President's 2026 disclosure values the licensor, DT Marks Mobile LLC, at $50,001 to $100,000 (its bank account and organizational costs only; the license is not valued) with income of less than $201 in 2025. Customers paid $100 deposits toward a $499 phone and $47.45 a month for service; the company has not said how many.

financial_stake.caveat: The disclosure covers calendar 2025, before the phone shipped in May 2026, so it does not show any royalties earned since; the license terms and any minimum guarantee are not public. Trump Mobile has not disclosed pre-order or subscriber counts "citing competitive reasons"; Ynet's estimate of roughly 590,000 deposits worth about $59 million is unconfirmed. The White House says the President's assets are in a trust managed by his children and "There are no conflicts of interest"; Trump's sons say they follow all "legal and ethical obligations." Carr says he learned of Trump Mobile from a press release and the FCC would follow its normal process; Trump Mobile says the delays came from quality testing and that it aims eventually to make a phone with mostly U.S. components.

legal_context: Lawful-but-concerning on the public record; no violation has been found. Lawmakers asked the FTC whether the made-in-USA marketing and the undelivered $100-deposit phones were deceptive or unfair practices, citing its Made in USA standard and a past Mail Order Rule settlement; the governing provisions are Section 5 of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 45), the Made in USA Labeling Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 323) and the Mail Order Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 435). The FTC has announced no investigation. The main federal conflict-of-interest statute, 18 U.S.C. 208, does not apply to the President (18 U.S.C. 202(c)).
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the launch, the licensing structure (Washington Post; the President's 2026 OGE disclosure), the dropped made-in-USA language (The Verge, CNBC), Carr's June 2025 statement (Reuters), the lawmakers' letters (primary PDFs and press releases) and the May 2026 shipping start (Reuters). The January 2026 FCC certification rests on CNET's account of The Verge's reading of FCC records; the HTC U24 Pro match rests on iFixit's teardown as reported by TechSpot, since NBC's own report was not read. The October 2026 data theft is a hacking group's claim, partly corroborated by PCMag. Sen. Hassan's October 8, 2026 letter is known through Techlicious and Straight Arrow News accounts; the letter itself was not read. No public figure shows how many phones were pre-ordered or shipped. MODERATE confidence on the government nexus: agencies led by the President's appointees oversee the venture, but no source shows any official act favored it, and the FTC's silence is documented only as an absence of public response. Re-verified 2026-10-29: no reply from Trump Mobile to Sen. Hassan's letter and no FCC or FTC action found as of her October 29 response deadline; PCMag quotes the letter directly, and Techlicious and Straight Arrow News still say what this entry cites.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Trump Mobile follows the Trump Organization's model of licensing the President's name to ventures run by others, the same model behind its Gulf and Vietnam real estate deals and the $TRUMP memecoin's licensing agreement. What sets it apart is that it sells into markets regulated by agencies whose leaders the President appoints and can remove, so routine approvals and enforcement choices about it are hard to separate from the family interest even where, as here, no favoritism has been shown.

glance.what: Trump-licensed phone venture dropped its made-in-USA claim and shipped late as Trump appointees oversaw it

section_summaries.what_changed: Trump's sons launched a Trump-licensed phone marketed as U.S.-made; it shipped nine months late as a reskinned HTC, while FCC and FTC chairs fielded conflict questions.
section_summaries.financial_stake: License terms are secret; Trump's 2026 disclosure shows the licensor earned under $201 in 2025, before phones shipped. Buyers paid $100 deposits on a $499 phone.

title: Trump's company signed foreign deals from the Gulf to Vietnam, Korea and Georgia, some with state-linked partners or a firm in a U.S. trade case, while he set policy toward them

business_entity.name: Trump Organization
business_entity.family_stake: The Trump Organization is owned by President Trump and led by his two eldest sons (The Hill); his assets are in a trust run by his children, who handle day-to-day operations while he is in office (AP), and income from the businesses ultimately accrues to the president (Reuters). Eric Trump, executive vice president, announced the Jeddah, Qatar, Diriyah and Maldives deals and attended the Vietnam groundbreaking (The Hill, Trump Organization, Zawya, eNCA/AFP). Forbes reported that Trump-owned entities created in November 2025 hold 80% of a Diriyah hotel management agreement, with family members, presumably Eric and Donald Jr., holding the remaining 20%.

government_nexus.action: As president, Trump made Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE his first major foreign trip in May 2025, signing a $600 billion Saudi commercial package with a nearly $142 billion defense sale and a Qatar 'economic exchange' worth at least $1.2 trillion; signed Executive Order 14353 guaranteeing Qatar's security (September 29, 2025); designated Saudi Arabia a major non-NATO ally and approved F-35 deliveries during the crown prince's November 2025 visit; set Vietnam's reciprocal tariff, which faced a threatened 46% and was held at 20% in an October 2025 trade framework; asked by Indonesia's president in October 2025 to set up a meeting with Eric Trump, replied 'I'll have Eric call you'; oversaw, through his Commerce Department, duty proceedings against a Korean firm whose parent paid his company $2 million in 2025; and opened his family's new Scottish course at the end of a July 2025 trip the White House called a 'working trip.'

also_officials.role: Minister of Municipality of Qatar and chairman of Qatari Diar

also_officials.name: Mohammed bin Salman
also_officials.role: Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia (chairs the Diriyah Company, per Forbes)

government_nexus.note: The deals' counterparties are tied to the governments Trump was negotiating with: Qatari Diar is a state-owned firm chaired by a Qatari minister (The Media Line); Diriyah and the other Saudi giga-projects are owned by the Saudi sovereign wealth fund (The New York Times, via The Boston Globe); and Dar Global, the partner on most Gulf deals, is a subsidiary of Saudi developer Dar Al Arkan with close ties to the Saudi government (same). Vietnam's prime minister pledged the Hung Yen project 'maximum support' to 'further strengthen the relationship between Vietnam and the U.S.' as tariff talks went on (The Independent), and the Diriyah CEO said Saudi officials showed Trump the site during his May 2025 state visit to 'appeal to him as a developer.' Base Group paid its $2 million while its affiliate was contesting Commerce duties (The New York Times via The New Republic), and the Tbilisi land came from a fund tied to a U.S.-sanctioned party leader whose allies were seeking better ties with Washington (The Wall Street Journal via JAMnews). No source reports that any U.S. policy decision was exchanged for a deal, and CNBC found no evidence the Vietnam project influenced tariff talks; the White House says the president's trade discussions are 'totally unrelated to the Trump Organization.'

status: Ongoing. Trump's 2025 disclosure showed $125 million from foreign golf and real estate. Trump Tower Tbilisi launched in September 2026, and senators are probing a Korean firm's $2 million fee as Commerce weighs final duties. No court has ruled; the White House denies any conflict.
date_of_action: 2024-12-11 (Trump Organization launches Trump Tower Jeddah as president-elect) through 2026-09-15 (Trump Tower Tbilisi launches in Georgia with the prime minister attending)
what_changed: On December 11, 2024, while his father was president-elect, Eric Trump launched the Trump Organization's first project in Saudi Arabia, a 47-floor Trump Tower in Jeddah with Dar Global, and the partners announced two more projects in Riyadh (The Hill). At Trump's January 2025 inauguration, heads of several foreign companies with Trump-branded projects, including Dar Global's CEO and its parent company's chairman, attended celebrations and touted their ties to his presidency; the company pledged no new deals directly with foreign governments, though it already had a project with Oman's state tourism arm (CNN). During the first term the company signed an ethics pact barring deals with foreign companies; the second-term framework allows them (AP). In March 2025 Vietnam's prime minister expressed support for expediting a Trump Organization project in a meeting with the head of a firm representing it in the country (CREW). In April 2025, in a virtual meeting with Israeli real estate executives, Eric Trump discussed a possible deal to manage and brand the Sarona hotel under construction in Tel Aviv, and said he planned to sign at least one deal in Israel by the end of the year (The New York Times, citing a person involved). On April 30, 2025, Qatari Diar, a state-owned developer chaired by Qatar's Minister of Municipality, signed an agreement with Dar Global to develop Trump International Golf Club, Doha, with Trump-branded villas, inside the $5.5 billion Simaisma development (Trump Organization; Reuters); the Trump Organization says its agreement is only with Dar Global (The Media Line). The same day Dar Global and the Trump Organization launched Trump International Hotel & Tower, Dubai, an 80-floor tower and their fifth collaboration (Dar Global release); The New York Times described the $1 billion tower, whose units went on sale after a party honoring Eric Trump, as part of a burst of deals by the president's two older sons that also included a second Jeddah tower, crypto ventures and a Washington club. On Trump's May 2025 Gulf trip, which began in Riyadh on May 13, the White House announced a $600 billion Saudi package including a nearly $142 billion defense sale and a Qatar agreement for an 'economic exchange' worth at least $1.2 trillion, and on his first night in Riyadh Trump toured Diriyah, the crown prince's $63 billion development, with Mohammed bin Salman (White House; The New York Times via The Boston Globe). On May 21, 2025, Eric Trump attended the groundbreaking of a $1.5 billion Trump golf resort in Hung Yen, Vietnam, with developer Kinhbac City, which paid the Trump Organization $5 million for licensing rights (eNCA/AFP; Reuters); The New York Times, as relayed by The Independent, reported that the project skipped environmental reviews and cut short public comment, and that a letter said it was 'receiving special attention from the Trump administration and President Donald Trump personally,' while Vietnam faced a threatened 46% U.S. tariff. After an Iranian missile struck the Sarona neighborhood on June 13, 2025, The New York Times reported the Tel Aviv talks on June 25; Eric Trump said 'any discussions have been strictly preliminary' and that the company had 'no plans at this time' in Israel. In July 2025 the company announced Trump Tower Bucharest with Romanian developer SDC Imobiliare (Bloomberg). From July 25 to 29, 2025 Trump visited Scotland, holding trade talks with British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and the European Union, and with Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. cut the ribbon on the family's new course at Balmedie, which was already selling tee times (AP; ABC). In August 2025 Reuters reported that farmers displaced for the Vietnam resort were being offered $12 to $30 per square meter plus rice. On September 29, 2025 Trump signed an executive order guaranteeing Qatar's security (Federal Register). On October 13, 2025, at the Gaza summit in Egypt, a live microphone caught Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto asking Trump, 'Can I meet Eric?' Trump replied, 'I'll have Eric call you,' and Prabowo added, 'Eric or Don Jr.'; Reuters noted it was not clear whether they meant the Trump Organization, which has golf and resort projects near Jakarta and in Bali with Indonesian partner MNC Group (Reuters via Malay Mail; Asia Sentinel). On October 16 Eric Trump said he had not met Prabowo and that 'I don't get involved in politics in Indonesia' (Yahoo News; Asia Sentinel). On October 26, 2025, the U.S.-Vietnam trade framework held Vietnam's reciprocal tariff at 20% (White House). On November 15, 2025, Diriyah's CEO told The New York Times a Trump-branded deal was 'just a matter of time'; on November 17 the company announced a tokenized Trump hotel in the Maldives with Dar Global (The Hill); that month a Trump representative created two companies that took an 80% stake in a Diriyah hotel management agreement (Forbes), and on November 18 Trump designated Saudi Arabia a major non-NATO ally and approved F-35 deliveries during the crown prince's White House visit (Al Jazeera). On November 27, 2025, the company's trademark arm applied for five trademarks in Vietnam for the Hung Yen project, the first foreign trademark applications CREW found in Trump's second term, filed months after the lower tariff rate was reached, CREW later reported (CREW). On January 11, 2026, Dar Al Arkan and Dar Global unveiled Trump International Golf Club, Wadi Safar, inside Diriyah (Zawya), part of two Saudi Trump projects worth a combined $10 billion (Enterprise, citing Reuters). On February 11, 2026, Eric Trump toured a development site in Hanam, South Korea, with Kim Sung-jip, chairman of Base Group, whose affiliate Korea Aluminium had been found by the Commerce Department in 2023 to be circumventing duties on Chinese aluminum (The Korea Times; Sen. Ron Wyden). On February 19, 2026, CREW projected, from his 2024 income and newly announced projects, that Trump's second-term income from overseas developments would exceed $400 million and likely top $430 million (CREW). On April 18, 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported plans for a 70-story Trump Tower Tbilisi in Georgia (Reuters via BusinessDay), and in May Georgian investors, including former Georgian Dream lawmaker Ilia Tsulaia, who had joined a 2025 Georgian delegation to Washington seeking better relations and discussing sanctions, signed a branding agreement with Eric Trump at Mar-a-Lago (The Wall Street Journal via JAMnews). In June 2026 the Financial Times, as relayed by Atlanta Black Star, reported that graves were being dug up for the Vietnam resort. Trump's 2025 financial disclosure, released June 30, 2026, showed about $2.24 billion in business revenue, with $125 million from foreign golf and real estate (The New York Times), around $300 million from Gulf entities across all his businesses (The Wall Street Journal, via Political Wire), and $38 million in Gulf real estate licensing fees (The National). In July 2026 a preliminary Commerce Department ruling could raise duties on Korea Aluminium's foil exports to as much as 105.8% (Asiae; The Korea Times), and on July 14 The New York Times reported that the disclosure listed a $2 million 'nonrefundable development fee' tied to a 'letter of intent' that Base Group paid Trump's holding company in 2025; Base Group and the Trump Organization said it was for an unannounced golf course and unrelated to the trade case, and the Times found no evidence the family advocated for the companies (The New Republic; Korea JoongAng Daily). The same month, developers of the Tbilisi tower completed a purchase, worth up to $85 million, of land bought from a fund controlled by the family of U.S.-sanctioned Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili (The Wall Street Journal via JAMnews). On July 20, 2026, CREW put Trump's 2025 revenue from overseas business at over $117 million, a record (CREW). Forbes reported on July 23, 2026 that further Trump companies tied to Saudi projects had been registered in 2026 but did not appear on the disclosure. On August 5, 2026, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal and Andy Kim wrote to Base Group's chairman asking whether the payment was meant to influence Commerce proceedings (Senate letter). On August 10, 2026, a CNBC analysis of the disclosure put Trump's 2025 foreign licensing income at $59.5 million, up 71% from 2024, and found no evidence the Vietnam project influenced the tariff talks. On August 13, 2026, Base Group and the Trump Organization announced Trump International Golf Club, Korea, in Hanam (Trump Organization), and on August 18 Sen. Ron Wyden asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for records on the Korea Aluminium case (Senate Finance Committee letter). On September 15, 2026, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze attended the launch of Trump Tower Tbilisi, a $2 billion development now marketed at 62 stories, and Eric Trump said by video that 'this all started at Mar-a-Lago' (The National; Georgia Today). Kushner's separate Belgrade project is covered in its own entry.

financial_stake.caveat: The revenue figures come from Trump's own disclosure forms as tallied by The New York Times, which used range minimums and notes the forms record his personal cut of revenue, not profit. The Wall Street Journal's $300 million Gulf figure covers all his businesses, not only real estate, and TAP read only its quoted summary. CREW's estimates use range minimums from the same forms. Project values ($1.5 billion, $5.5 billion, $10 billion, Tbilisi's $2 billion) and the Tbilisi land price are developers' totals, not the family's take. The White House says Trump 'was a massively successful businessman prior to becoming president' and that there are no conflicts of interest; it said his trade talks are 'totally unrelated to the Trump Organization,' called the Scotland swing a 'working trip,' and Trump says 'I don't get involved' in his finances. Reuters reports the Trump Organization is not involved in the Vietnam investment or farmers' compensation, Base Group and the Trump Organization say the $2 million was for a golf course, announced in August 2026, and 'pure fiction' to suggest otherwise, and Commerce's July 2026 preliminary ruling went against the Korean firm; Eric Trump says the Indonesia projects long predate his father's candidacy and called the Israel talks 'strictly preliminary'; and the company says the Diriyah hotel deal was not finalized at the same time as the president's nuclear talks.

legal_context: Lawful-but-concerning as far as is known. The Foreign Emoluments Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, sec. 9, cl. 8) bars federal officeholders from accepting any present or emolument from a foreign state without the consent of Congress; attorneys have warned Trump's foreign business arrangements risk violating it (CNN), and two of these deals have state-owned counterparts (Qatari Diar; the Saudi sovereign fund's Diriyah project). The Trump Organization says its agreements are with the private developer Dar Global. The Supreme Court dismissed first-term emoluments suits as moot in 2021 without ruling on the merits (CNN; CNBC), and no court has ruled on these second-term deals. Senators asking Base Group about its $2 million payment cited the federal bribery statute, 18 U.S.C. 201, without alleging a violation, and no finding has been made; licensing a brand to foreign developers is not in itself illegal.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the deals themselves (Trump Organization and developer releases, Reuters, Bloomberg, AFP, The Hill), the official acts (White House fact sheets, the Federal Register, Al Jazeera) and the disclosure figures (The New York Times, The National). MODERATE confidence on the Tel Aviv talks (The New York Times, partly from an unnamed participant), the Base Group payment and the Tbilisi land deal, read through other outlets' accounts of The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal; Tbilisi's height was first reported as 70 stories and later marketed as 62. TAP found no report of a signed Israel deal or of a final Commerce ruling on Korea Aluminium. Disputed: whether any deal influenced U.S. policy. No source reports an explicit exchange, the White House denies any link, and this entry presents the timing as documented context, not proof.

title: Media companies Trump sued paid tens of millions to a library foundation run by his family, on state land the Trump Organization is developing as a possible hotel

business_entity.name: Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation, with the Trump Organization developing the project
business_entity.family_stake: Eric Trump, an executive vice president of the Trump Organization, and Michael Boulos, Tiffany Trump's husband, are two of the foundation's three trustees (the third is Trump attorney James Kiley). Eric Trump says he developed the project with his "incredible team" at the Trump Organization, which President Trump owns, and the President has said the building will "most likely" be a hotel. The foundation owns the Miami parcel; no contract between it and the Trump Organization has been disclosed.

government_nexus.action: As President-elect and then President, Trump accepted settlements of his own lawsuits that routed media companies' money to his library, including Paramount's $16 million while its Skydance merger awaited FCC approval; the foundation took a $50 million SoftBank gift two months before the Energy and Commerce Departments announced a SoftBank data center on federal land. Gov. Ron DeSantis and the Florida Cabinet deeded a state college parcel appraised at about $67 million to the foundation for $10.
government_nexus.note: Money from companies with business before the administration (Paramount while its merger awaited approval; SoftBank two months before its federal data-center lease was announced) flowed to a foundation that the President's son and son-in-law run, for a Trump-branded tower that the Trump Organization is developing and that the President says will most likely be a hotel. Plaintiffs in a pending federal suit say the free state land is an unconstitutional benefit to the President; the defendants say the foundation's charter bars private benefit and there is no proof the building will benefit Trump in office, and a supporting amicus brief says the land went to a separate nonprofit, not to Trump. No source shows a settlement or gift was exchanged for an official act, and no source has yet shown money flowing from the foundation to the Trump Organization.

status: Pending: in a federal Domestic Emoluments Clause suit over the Miami land gift, motions to dismiss were fully briefed Oct. 1, 2026, and discovery is stayed pending a ruling. The foundation has disclosed no donors or public answer on up to $14.5M in settlement money; construction has not begun.
date_of_action: 2024-12 (ABC agrees to pay $15 million toward Trump's library to settle his defamation suit) through 2026-10-08 (Boston Globe reports the foundation still has disclosed no donors as the federal land suit remains pending)
what_changed: On December 14, 2024, ABC News agreed to pay $15 million toward President-elect Trump's future presidential library, plus $1 million in legal fees to his lawyer, to settle his defamation suit over George Stephanopoulos's on-air statement about the E. Jean Carroll case; a nonprofit, the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Fund Inc., was set up that month. In January 2025, Meta agreed to pay $25 million to settle Trump's suit over the suspension of his Facebook and Instagram accounts after January 6, 2021; the Wall Street Journal reported that $22 million would go toward his library fund. In February 2025, Trump settled his suit against Elon Musk's X for about $10 million, according to a person familiar with the confidential deal who told the Associated Press that some of the money was expected to go to legal fees, with the balance directed to the library; the Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar, reported that Trump's share was expected to go to him directly. In May 2025, a second nonprofit with nearly the same mission, the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation Inc., was incorporated in Florida; its three trustees are Eric Trump, the President's son and an executive vice president of the Trump Organization, Michael Boulos, the husband of Tiffany Trump, and James Kiley, an attorney for the President. In June 2025, Florida enacted a law barring local regulation of any presidential library. On July 2, 2025, Paramount agreed to pay $16 million to settle Trump's suit over a "60 Minutes" interview with Kamala Harris, with the money going to the library; the Associated Press noted that Trump's administration had to approve Paramount's pending merger with Skydance, which the FCC approved on July 24, 2025. That month, Sen. Elizabeth Warren released a report counting at least $63 million pledged to the library by companies seeking favorable outcomes from the administration, and Democrats introduced the Presidential Library Anti-Corruption Act to limit library donations. In September 2025, days before the college vote, Florida administratively dissolved the original library fund after it failed to file an annual report. On September 23, 2025, Miami Dade College's trustees voted at an 8 a.m. special meeting, noticed only as a discussion of "potential real estate transactions," to give a 2.63-acre parking lot next to the Freedom Tower in downtown Miami to the state at Gov. Ron DeSantis's request; Attorney General James Uthmeier posted a video promoting the library site at 8:22 a.m. that day, and a week later DeSantis and the Florida Cabinet voted unanimously to deed the land, appraised at about $67 million, to the Trump library foundation. On October 14, 2025, Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Mavel Ruiz temporarily blocked the transfer in a suit by historian Marvin Dunn, finding the college had not given reasonable public notice. In an October 2025 filing with Florida charity regulators, reported by the New York Times on November 18, the foundation, headquartered at a Trump golf course in Jupiter, Florida, said it expected to raise about $50 million in its first year, budgeted $400,000 for officers including Eric Trump and Michael Boulos while stating in a separate filing that none would be paid, and listed a $6.2 million item, about 90% of planned spending, only as "other." On December 2, 2025, the college trustees held a second, fully noticed vote and again approved the transfer unanimously; on December 18, Judge Ruiz dismissed Dunn's suit, writing that the court was not deciding "whether this is wise." In January 2026, SoftBank Group gave $50 million to the library project, according to SoftBank's later response to Democratic lawmakers, who called it the largest publicly reported gift to the library. In February 2026, records reviewed by local media showed the state had transferred the parcel to the foundation for $10, with a deed condition that construction on a presidential library, museum and/or center start within five years. In March 2026, Sens. Warren and Richard Blumenthal and Rep. Melanie Stansbury wrote to ABC, Meta, X and Paramount asking where their settlement money had gone after the original fund's dissolution; ABC later told them its payment had sat in an escrow account set up by Trump's lawyers until at least March 2026, when the IRS recognized the foundation's tax-exempt status and Trump's attorneys asked for its release. On March 20, 2026, the Energy and Commerce Departments announced a partnership letting SoftBank build a data center of up to 10 gigawatts on federal land. On March 30, 2026, Eric Trump posted a "first look" video of a skyscraper bearing the Trump name, with a jet in its lobby, a golden escalator and a gold Trump statue, writing that over the past six months he had "poured my heart and soul into this project with my incredible team" at the Trump Organization, which reposted the message. The next day, President Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, "I don't believe in building libraries or museums," and that the building "could be [an] office, but it's most likely going to be a hotel with a beautiful building underneath and a 747 Air Force One in the lobby." In April 2026, the lawmakers released the companies' responses, which gave no public account of where most of the settlement money went, and wrote to the President asking why the foundation had been "preferred instead of the fund." In May 2026, a Miami nonprofit led by Dunn, two nearby residents and a Miami Dade College student, represented by the Constitutional Accountability Center and Gelber Schachter & Greenberg, sued Trump, the foundation, DeSantis, the college and other state officials in federal court in Miami (Sistrunk Seeds Inc. v. Trump), arguing that the land gift violates the Constitution's Domestic Emoluments Clause and would "house a Trump hotel that brings riches to the President"; on May 22, Politico first reported SoftBank's $50 million gift. Trump's 2025 financial disclosure, released June 30, 2026, listed settlements from Meta ($24.5 million), ABC ($16 million) and Paramount ($16 million) totaling $56.5 million with net proceeds going to the foundation, plus $8 million from X without saying where it went. On July 1, 2026, Warren, Blumenthal and Stansbury opened an inquiry into the SoftBank gift, and on July 16 they wrote to the foundation's treasurer that its $50 million in reported revenue left between $6.5 million and $14.5 million of settlement money unaccounted for, and asked it to explain nearly $7 million in expenses, about $6 million of them listed only as "other," and whether Trump or any family member had been paid. On August 6, 2026, the lawmakers released SoftBank's response confirming that its $50 million gift was made in January 2026, two months before the federal data-center lease was announced; a SoftBank lawyer said the company also supported other presidential libraries and that the gift would help create a space "highlighting the strength of the U.S.-Japan relationship." In August 2026, the Justice Department for Trump, and the state defendants and the foundation jointly, moved to dismiss the federal suit, arguing among other things that the plaintiffs lack standing; on August 31, the state defendants and the foundation, joined by Trump, asked U.S. District Judge Rodolfo Ruiz II to halt discovery. On September 8, the plaintiffs opposed the stay, saying they sought only limited discovery from the foundation, which they said does not claim immunity; on September 11, Judge Ruiz stayed all discovery until he rules on the motions to dismiss, citing the defendants' immunity defenses and standing challenges. The plaintiffs opposed dismissal on September 15, and the defendants replied on October 1. On October 8, 2026, the Boston Globe reported that the library would occupy the lower levels of a 47-story tower that Trump has said would mostly be a hotel or office space, with construction costing at least $950 million in tax-deductible contributions, and that the foundation had disclosed nothing about its donors.

financial_stake.summary: Four media and tech companies Trump sued agreed to pay about $63 million toward his library, by press accounts; his own disclosure lists $56.5 million from three of them paid to the foundation. SoftBank added $50 million. Florida gave the foundation land appraised at about $67 million for $10. The tower is to cost at least $950 million and may be mostly a hotel.
